Affordability. The affordability of insulins was expressed as the number of days’ wages (NDWs) required for a lowest-paid government employee to buy the 10 ml insulin, i.e., approximately a month’s supply. The salary was taken as 32000PKR per month (with effect from July 2023) [ ]. According to the WHO/HAI benchmark, if a patient has to spend more than 1 day’s wage for treatment with a specific medicine in a month, that medicine is considered unaffordable. 2.5.4. Availability. The availability was measured as percentage availability, considering the number of retail pharmacies with a particular insulin product available on the day of data collection. The following is a description of the % availability: absent, meaning that at the time of the survey, none of the surveyed pharmacies stocked the specific insulin product; fairly low, meaning that the insulin product was present in less than 30% of facilities; low, meaning that it was present in fewer than 50% of facilities; fairly high, meaning that between 50% and 80% of facilities had the insulin product; high, meaning that the majority of the facilities had the insulin [ ]. The availability analysis consisted of data from the post-implementation period of the deregulation policy. These analyses were performed using Microsoft Excel and Stata (version 15; StataCorp LLC, College Station, TX, USA). All descriptive results were presented following standard WHO/HAI reporting categories to maintain consistency with international medicine price and availability surveys. 2.6. Ethical approval and consent to participate Ethical approval was obtained from the ethical review committee of the pharmacy practice department, Bahauddin Zakariya University, Multan, Pakistan (Letter no. BZU-FOPDPP-2455). The study did not involve patients or the collection of personal or identifiable data; only publicly available maximum retail prices of insulin products were collected from sampled private retail pharmacies. Verbal informed consent was obtained from the pharmacists or pharmacy managers before data collection. 2.7. Inclusivity in global research Additional information regarding the ethical, cultural, and scientific considerations specific to inclusivity in global research is included in the Supporting Information ( ). 3. Results 3.1. Insulin prices by product characteristics The median insulin price (per 10 mL) increased significantly following deregulation, rising from PKR 2030 (7.3 USD) to 2678 (9.6 USD), representing a 31.9% increase (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p < 0.001). By NEML-enlistment status, NEML insulins were consistently priced lower than non-NEML insulins both before (PKR 1035 vs. 3367) and after deregulation (PKR 1267 vs. 4622); however, post-deregulation price increases were larger among non-NEML insulins (37.2%) than NEML-listed insulins (22.2%) ( p < 0.001) ( ). When stratified by origin, analogue insulins were consistently priced higher than human insulins both before and after deregulation. Median prices of human insulins increased from PKR 975.0 to 1230.5, while analogue insulin prices rose from PKR 4288.6 to 5336.6 ( p < 0.001) ( ). In terms of duration of action, the intermediate-acting human insulins experienced the highest price hike, by 30%. Among the insulin analogues, Lispro (a rapid-acting analogue) experienced the highest price increase of 28%, rising from PKR 3367.30 to 4622.0 post deregulation ( ). Product-wise, OBs were priced substantially higher than BS both before and after deregulation and experienced a marked price increase from PKR 3746.6 to 4626.6 ( p < 0.001). In contrast, BS showed no change in median price, remaining at PKR 900. Among presentation types, prefilled pens were priced higher than cartridges and vials at both time points, increasing from PKR 4396.6 to 5342.0, compared with cartridges (PKR 3246.6 to 4622.0) and vials (PKR 975.0 to 1096.8). The prefilled pens exhibited the highest price increase (42.2%), followed by cartridges (24.6%) and vials (19.7%). 3.2. Differential effect of deregulation on insulin prices: DiD analysis presents the findings from the DiD analysis. Both models showed significant price hikes among non-NEML insulins post-deregulation. In model 1 (without confounders), the DiD interaction term showed a differential increase of PKR 998 (p < 0.001), which further increased to PKR 1142 (p < 0.001) after adjusting for insulin characteristics, indicating that non-NEML products were disproportionately impacted by the policy. Furthermore, both models confirmed that the prices of insulins were significantly higher overall after deregulation by

pens exhibited the highest price increase (42.2%), followed by cartridges (24.6%) and vials (19.7%). 3.2. Differential effect of deregulation on insulin prices: DiD analysis presents the findings from the DiD analysis. Both models showed significant price hikes among non-NEML insulins post-deregulation. In model 1 (without confounders), the DiD interaction term showed a differential increase of PKR 998 (p < 0.001), which further increased to PKR 1142 (p < 0.001) after adjusting for insulin characteristics, indicating that non-NEML products were disproportionately impacted by the policy. Furthermore, both models confirmed that the prices of insulins were significantly higher overall after deregulation by PKR 1379.2 ( p < 0.001) than they were before. The baseline price gap between NEML and non-NEML insulins (PKR –2509; p < 0.001) became statistically insignificant after adjustment, reflecting that observed differences were largely explained by product attributes. Among covariates in the adjusted model, OBs were more expensive than biosimilars (PKR 374.8; p < 0.001), analogue insulins were markedly costlier than human insulins (PKR 3131.6; p < 0.001), and prefilled pens were more expensive than vials (PKR 257.8; p < 0.05). The adjusted model demonstrated substantially improved model fit (R² = 0.80 vs. 0.40), indicating that accounting for insulin characteristics greatly increased explanatory power. 3.3. Affordability After deregulation, the affordability was significantly reduced, particularly for OB analogue insulins. Within six months of the deregulation policy’s launch, the median NDWs increased from 1.9 days before deregulation to 2.5 days after it, a 32% decline in the overall affordability of insulins ( ). Only the BS insulins remained affordable both before and after deregulation, with the NDWs remaining static at 0.8. Contrarily, the OB insulins remained unaffordable at both time points, showing a 73% decrease in affordability. In the human versus analogue comparison of affordability, human insulins remained marginally affordable; however, they did show a reduction in affordability by 26%. On the other hand, the analogue insulins remained unaffordable pre- and post-deregulation, with 4 and 5 NDWs, respectively, a reduction in affordability by 25%. Among analogue insulins, particularly the long-acting analogues of OB, such as detemir and glargine, highly unaffordable levels were observed, exceeding 5 days’ wages per 10 ml. Notably, the mixed analogue formulation, i.e., Aspart/Degludec was the least affordable with more than 10 NDWs post-deregulation. Among the specific insulin products, OBs of intermediate-acting human insulin and Lispro (a rapid acting insulin analogue) showed a substantial reduction in affordability, i.e., by 30% and 37%, respectively ( ). When stratified by presentation type, although all types experienced an increase in the NDWs, vials remained relatively affordable in both periods, i.e., 0.9 and 1.0 NDWs. Meanwhile, the prefilled pens and cartridges remained unaffordable at both time points, resulting in a 25% and 42% reduction in affordability. 3.4. Post-deregulation availability of insulin Overall, OB insulins were more widely available than BS, with 78.0% of human and 48.8% of analogue insulins available as OBs, compared to 51.1% and only 8.3% as BS insulins, respectively. This trend highlights how OBs continue to dominate the market, even for insulin types with BS substitutes ( ). OB Glargine, a long-acting insulin analogue, was found to be the highest available insulin type (90%) ( ). Besides glargine, only OBs of isophane and 70/30 (isophane/regular) had the ideal availability, i.e., 80%. OB glulisine had very low availability (<30%), while degludec was not found in the market. BS products of insulin regular, isophane, 70/30 (isophane/regular), and glargine were found to have fairly high availability of 50%, 53.3%, and 50%, respectively ( ). 3.5. Market composition of insulin products A total of 380 insulin products (including duplicates) were found in the private sector market ( ). 48% (n = 184) of these were human insulin products and 52% (n = 196) were analogue insulins. 85% of these products was manufactured by three MNCs i.e., Eli Lilly (39%), Novo Nordisk (34%), and Sanofi Aventis (12%). However, only 15% of these products were manufactured collectively by local manufacturers. The share of available insulin products by presentation type was Vial>Prefilled Pen>Cartridge. The NEML insulins (65%) were relatively more available than non-NEML enlisted insulins (35%). 3.6. City-wise average number of insulin products per pharmacy All surveyed outlets had at least one insulin product available. However, the average number of products available at retail pharmacies varied across different regions and ranged from 5 in Quetta (Baluchistan) to 20 in Lahore (Punjab)( and ). 4. Discussion To the best of our knowledge, this is the first national study to empirically assess the impact of Pakistan’s recent medicine price deregulation policy on insulin prices and affordability using a quasi-experimental approach. Additionally, it presents national-scale insights into insulin access in private retail pharmacies across the country. After deregulation, the prices of nearly all categories of insulin experienced a significant hike, particularly in OBs, analogues, and prefilled pens. The overall

the average number of products available at retail pharmacies varied across different regions and ranged from 5 in Quetta (Baluchistan) to 20 in Lahore (Punjab)( and ). 4. Discussion To the best of our knowledge, this is the first national study to empirically assess the impact of Pakistan’s recent medicine price deregulation policy on insulin prices and affordability using a quasi-experimental approach. Additionally, it presents national-scale insights into insulin access in private retail pharmacies across the country. After deregulation, the prices of nearly all categories of insulin experienced a significant hike, particularly in OBs, analogues, and prefilled pens. The overall insulin price increase of 32% post-deregulation in an LMIC like Pakistan is particularly concerning [ , ]. Notably, about 85% of all medical expenses in Pakistan are spent at private facilities, indicating the country’s heavy reliance on the private sector [ ]. Thus, the current study—which focuses on insulin access in private sector settings—is particularly relevant and crucial for guiding evidence-based policy and enhancing equitable access to these essential diabetes treatments. Although BS human insulins did not exhibit price increases, their market availability was comparatively limited. While the overall affordability of insulin for those on low wages was found to be poor, both before and after deregulation, it was reported to have been significantly reduced further within just six months of the policy’s launch. However, insulin availability was found to be moderate to high for most insulin products post-deregulation. 4.1. Insulin prices by product characteristics The analogue insulins were at substantially higher prices than human insulins at both time points. This finding aligns with the observations from not only LMICs but also HICs(7). For instance, the prices of insulin analogues have been reported to be ten times higher than those of regular or NPH human insulins in the US [ ]. Before deregulation, the OB prices were approximately 4.2 times higher than BS and increased to 5.2 times higher after deregulation. A previous study conducted in 2019 reported this difference to be much less in Pakistan, i.e., OBs were priced 1.34 times higher than BS insulins [ ]. This widening price gap suggests increasing potential for cost savings through greater use of BS insulins. Notably, price increases were observed primarily among OBs, while BS prices remained stable. The static and lower prices of BS products may reflect competitive pressures from MNCs and limited market share, as observed in several other LMICs [ , ]. Among the human insulins, the intermediate-acting insulins, i.e., Isophane (NPH), showed the highest price increment. This finding is particularly concerning as NPH is not only part of the NEML but also one of the most frequently prescribed insulins globally and is considered an affordable option for cost-sensitive patients [ ]. Among the analogue insulins, Lispro underwent the largest price increase (28%), followed by Aspart and Glargine. Although all analogues were high-priced, the relatively lower price increment in glargine may be partly attributable to the presence of its BS product in the market. A study conducted in 28 European countries reported a significant price reduction for the originator glargine after the entry of BS glargine in the markets [ ]. Among the various presentations, prefilled pens experienced the highest price hike following deregulation. Although the use of prefilled insulin pens is comparatively less prevalent in LMICs, their high prices have caused great concern in developed countries where their use is frequent [ ]. 4.2. Impact of deregulation on insulin prices: insights from Difference-in-Differences analysis The findings from the adjusted DiD model revealed that the prices of non-NEML insulins increased disproportionately compared to those listed on the NEML. This may be attributed to the poor market competition for insulin in Pakistan, where a few MNCs, like several other LMICs(7). Importantly, the DiD estimates isolate the differential price change associated with deregulation after accounting for baseline differences and product characteristics, strengthening the interpretation that non-NEML insulins were more strongly affected by the policy change. The deregulation might have enabled oligopolistic pricing practices for this already high-priced medicine, further restricting its affordability. A study conducted in China to gauge the effect of deregulation policy on drug prices found similar results, stating that price changes after policy implementation varied among drug categories [ ]. It is also noteworthy that although the price deregulation was employed for the non-NEML medicines, the prices of NEML insulins, particularly OBs, were also increased. Liu et al. also found that the cost of essential medications had increased significantly, affecting low-income groups [ ], following the implementation of the medicine price deregulation. This suggests that price deregulation, even if aimed at non-NEML medications, may have wider market effects and result in unexpected price hikes for essential medicines as well. The persistently poor availability of BS products in the market would be a great challenge in realizing these

categories [ ]. It is also noteworthy that although the price deregulation was employed for the non-NEML medicines, the prices of NEML insulins, particularly OBs, were also increased. Liu et al. also found that the cost of essential medications had increased significantly, affecting low-income groups [ ], following the implementation of the medicine price deregulation. This suggests that price deregulation, even if aimed at non-NEML medications, may have wider market effects and result in unexpected price hikes for essential medicines as well. The persistently poor availability of BS products in the market would be a great challenge in realizing these savings. In the unadjusted model, NEML insulins were significantly cheaper than non-NEML insulins. After accounting for product characteristics, the difference became statistically insignificant. This suggests that the lower prices of NEML insulins are largely attributable to the types of products listed on the NEML rather than the NEML inclusion itself. 4.3. Insulin affordability Despite differences across product types, affordability remained poor for most insulin categories both before and after deregulation, with a further deterioration observed after the policy. This indicates that price increases directly translated into increased financial burden for patients, particularly those dependent on OBs and analogue insulins. These results are in line with previous evidence from Pakistan, where a 2019 study indicated these products to be unaffordable. Similar findings have also been reported in two states of India, where Sharma et al. and Satheesh et al. documented comparable challenges in the private sector [ , ]. Notably, both Pakistan and India still struggle with low affordability, even though India has more domestic insulin production capacity than Pakistan. This shows that local manufacturing may not be enough to guarantee access to affordable BS insulin products, particularly when MNC products are more frequently stocked and preferred by patients and providers [ ]. Only the human BS insulin remained marginally affordable, i.e., NDW < 1, at both time points. This finding is opposite to the one in our previous study conducted five years ago, where all insulin products were found unaffordable (NDW > 1), including human BS insulins. This suggests that human BS insulin has become slightly more affordable over time, either as a result of improved minimum wages, price changes, or heightened market competition. 4.4. Insulin availability As availability data were collected only post-deregulation, the findings in this section describe current market availability rather than the causal effects of the deregulation policy. Pakistan’s insulin market is dominated by a few MNCs exerting significant market control. Our data indicated that local manufacturers predominantly produce human insulin formulations, regular insulin, isophane (NPH), and premixed isophane/regular (70/30), mainly supplied as 100 IU/mL vials, while production of insulin analogues is limited to a single long-acting analogue (glargine), largely available as prefilled pens; moreover, domestic production is concentrated among a small number of firms, suggesting limited diversification into analogue and combination products. After deregulation, the overall insulin availability in private pharmacies of Pakistan was found to be moderate to high. Notably, only OBs of Glargine and isophane/regular (70/30) had availability above the WHO’s benchmark of 80%. This finding was contrary to findings from our study in 2019, where none of the insulin products had availability above 80% [ ]. Although this suggests improvement in the availability of these products over time, this change cannot be directly associated with deregulation policy, as city-level availability data were not collected in the current study. However, recent news reports and interviews with representatives of the Pakistan Pharmaceutical Manufacturers’ Association suggest that deregulation has improved drug availability, with a reported 21.7% growth in market value driven by new launches, line extensions, and the return of hardship products [ ]. Though the pharmaceutical manufacturing businesses may have benefited overall from this policy, there is no funding or policy to preserve patients’ affordability, particularly for those with low incomes, for expensive and frequently prescribed medications to treat highly prevalent diseases such as diabetes. Besides, clarifying the causal relationship between policy changes and insulin availability will require future longitudinal research with more detailed data. It appears that Pakistan’s insulin market, like those in several developing countries, is witnessing a shift from human insulin to analogue insulin, as the only insulin product with the highest availability (90%) was OB of a long-acting insulin analogue glargine [ , , ]. Whereas in 2019, none of the analogue insulins had availability beyond 80%. The availability of BS glargine also improved from <30% to 50%. Similarly, the availability of OBs of insulin aspart and detemir also improved. On the other hand, compared to 2019, the availability of human insulin products stayed somewhat similar. The increasing use of analogue insulin formulations is possibly the reason for the rise in their availability in Pakistan’s private sector between 2019 and 2024 [ ]. Notably, the clinical efficacy of costlier insulin

highest availability (90%) was OB of a long-acting insulin analogue glargine [ , , ]. Whereas in 2019, none of the analogue insulins had availability beyond 80%. The availability of BS glargine also improved from <30% to 50%. Similarly, the availability of OBs of insulin aspart and detemir also improved. On the other hand, compared to 2019, the availability of human insulin products stayed somewhat similar. The increasing use of analogue insulin formulations is possibly the reason for the rise in their availability in Pakistan’s private sector between 2019 and 2024 [ ]. Notably, the clinical efficacy of costlier insulin analogues, which increase the financial burden on healthcare systems and patients, is still debated [ ]. Analog insulin helps lower hypoglycemic episodes and weight gain, improve treatment adherence, lessen anxiety over dose adjustments, and increase patient satisfaction, according to evidence primarily from higher-income nations [25,27]. Conversely, only 23% of the 64 comparison trials reviewed indicated that analogues were more effective at reducing A1C levels [ ]. Therefore, the growing availability of analogue insulins in Pakistan poses significant concerns regarding cost-effectiveness and equitable access in a healthcare system with limited resources, even as it reflects changing clinical preferences and market realities. Another notable shift in the insulin availability over the past five years was the decline in the availability of vial formulations and the increase in the availability of high-cost prefilled pens, similar to those in several other countries [ , , ]. In 2019, the vials accounted for 58.4% of all insulin products in the market, which dropped to 44% by 2024. Conversely, the percentage of prefilled pens rose from 29.6% to 36%, indicating a steady shift toward more convenient but more costly delivery devices [ ]. Since analogue insulin pens and cartridges are more costly than human insulin vials, such a shift will have a significant financial impact on the local healthcare system. As per our findings, the lowest-paid unskilled worker in Pakistan would have to pay 1.03 days’ wage to get the vial formulations compared to 5.04 days’ wage to get the prefilled pen. Furthermore, patients with diabetes pay considerably more to address comorbidities. We found that all surveyed pharmacies across six cities had at least one insulin product available, indicating a baseline level of market presence. However, possible regional disparities in insulin accessibility were highlighted by the noteworthy variations in the average number of stocked insulin products, ranging from 5 in Quetta (Baluchistan) to 20 in Lahore (Punjab). These discrepancies reflect geographical variations in insulin demand, economic development, and health infrastructure. The availability was significantly higher in cities like Lahore and Islamabad, which are located in more developed provinces with better health systems, higher health budgets, and more affluent populations [ ]. Quetta’s restricted access, on the other hand, might be due to a smaller population size and underfunding of Baluchistan’s healthcare system, which is in line with the region’s lower Human Development Index and subpar healthcare delivery [ ]. On the other hand, insulin availability varied among pharmacies in major cities such as Karachi, a sign of inefficient supply chains and irregular stocking procedures. These results suggest that region-specific efforts and a fairer distribution method are needed to enhance insulin access across the country. 4.5. Policy implications While multiple factors may have influenced insulin price changes over the past two years, our findings indicate that the deregulation policy was associated with disproportionately higher price increases for non-NEML insulins. The finding that non-NEML insulins experienced larger price increases than NEML-listed products underscore the importance of reassessing the use of NEML status as the sole criterion for price deregulation. A more nuanced approach could be considered by policymakers, especially for diabetes treatments like insulin that are supplied through a highly concentrated market. The stable prices of BS insulins signify their competitive potential. Therefore, there is a dire need to promote market competition by supporting the local insulin manufacturers through targeted interventions such as investment in local production, pricing incentives, technology transfer, and a streamlined registration process. In order to build public trust and encourage the acceptance of locally produced BS insulins, their efficacy and safety must be compared with those of MNCs, and results must be shared and promoted publicly. Literature shows that the entry of BS insulins has led to significant price reductions of expensive analogues such as glargine [ ], and the efficacy of these products is comparable [ ]. Pakistani insulin manufacturers partner with the government to promote the public health advantages of less expensive human insulin and biosimilars as part of their corporate social duty. The amplified use of insulin analogues and prefilled pens, despite limited evidence on superior efficacy, emphasizes the need for the implementation of policy tools such as prescription evaluations and health technology assessment to guide the cost-effective use. The use

promoted publicly. Literature shows that the entry of BS insulins has led to significant price reductions of expensive analogues such as glargine [ ], and the efficacy of these products is comparable [ ]. Pakistani insulin manufacturers partner with the government to promote the public health advantages of less expensive human insulin and biosimilars as part of their corporate social duty. The amplified use of insulin analogues and prefilled pens, despite limited evidence on superior efficacy, emphasizes the need for the implementation of policy tools such as prescription evaluations and health technology assessment to guide the cost-effective use. The use of analogues must also be restricted by devising and implementing evidence-based guidelines prioritizing the use of less expensive and quality-assured human insulins. After deregulation, the spillover effects, evident from the indirect price increases observed in NEML insulins, although lower than those of non-NEML products, highlight the need for a strong and continuous medicine price monitoring system. There is a need to implement targeted insurance plans or subsidies to protect the vulnerable groups from incurring catastrophic health spending. 4.6. Limitations Despite the advantages and reliability of WHO/HAI methodology for measuring access to medicines and DID analysis for policy evaluation [ , ], there are some limitations. First, the DiD analysis was limited due to the availability of price data from only two time points, and including additional time points would have enhanced the reliability and robustness of the findings. Nevertheless, the adjusted DiD model showed a statistically significant effect, with a higher R², indicating improved fit and greater precision by accounting for insulin characteristics. Subsequent studies should expand the dataset and include variables such as manufacturers’ policies and retailer behavior to provide a more detailed analysis. Second, there could be variations compared to actual market prices before deregulation; however, the pre-deregulation (published) prices were obtained from a reliable and well-known source for retrospective study [ – ]. Third, we were only able to evaluate post-deregulation data for insulin availability in this study. Comparing it to our 2019 survey, however, gave helpful background information and, over time, showed significant trends. Finally, the study did not include the prices and availability data from public sector hospitals; however, the medicines are provided free of cost in the public sector of Pakistan, and insulin is not provided in outpatient pharmacies. Therefore, patients predominantly obtain insulin from retail pharmacies, which were therefore exclusively analyzed to assess the impact of deregulation on insulin prices and affordability. 5. Conclusion This study reveals the unintended consequences of Pakistan’s first-ever medicine price deregulation policy on insulin access, which include significant price hikes and decreased affordability, especially for underprivileged groups managing chronic conditions like diabetes. Although the goal of deregulation was to increase market efficiency, it highlights the need for a more focused strategy that protects access to life-saving medications in concentrated markets such as insulins. Regular price monitoring, promotion of locally produced insulins, and judicious price control mechanisms can increase competition and guarantee equitable access. To balance market dynamics with public health priorities, policymakers need to reevaluate the criteria for medicine price deregulation. chunks.content: Introduction The overdose crisis in the US continues to worsen with increasing tolls of overdoses on individuals and communities ( ). Overdoses are increasing due to the volatility of the illicit drug supply, emerging drugs such as xylazine (a tranquilizer that is increasingly mixed with opioids), ubiquity of fentanyl and its analogs, and continued barriers to treatment and harm reduction services ( ; ). Studies on the experience of opioid overdoses date back to 1999 ( ). More recently, studies have investigated the experience of those responding to overdoses, showing the impact of repeated overdose response on emergency medical personnel including burnout, exhaustion, compassion fatigue, and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) ( ; ). The growing national recognition of the impact of overdoses on first responders has resulted in formalized support systems for professionals responding to overdoses ( ; ; ). However, less support is available for people who use drugs, who often respond to overdoses ahead (or instead) of emergency personnel, and experience frequent and cumulative loss due to overdose among peers ( ; ). The act of responding to overdose, a “life-or-death” situation, has been documented as a potential source of trauma for people who use drugs, as it is for emergency personnel ( ; ; ). Between 70–79 % of people who inject drugs have witnessed an overdose in their lifetime ( ; ; ), and many reported witnessing overdose(s) in the recent past ( ; ). This trauma may be particularly acute for those who are not trained medical professionals and those at personal risk of overdose, and it is exacerbated by the lack of follow-up services for lay first responders. Moreover, people who use drugs experience barriers to accessing mental health and other support services ( ) that could help them cope with this trauma. Witnessing overdoses is associated with meeting diagnostic criteria for PTSD ( ; ; ) and PTSD is associated with experiencing a nonfatal overdose ( ). Understanding the bidirectional relationship between trauma and overdose and ensuring adequate systems and supports are in place for people who use drugs who respond to overdoses that are living with the aftermath of these experiences is critical. Prior qualitative studies based in the US and internationally describe experiences of overdose response among people who use drugs and have found emotional reactions (e.g., confidence, guilt, anxiety, burnout, grief), behavioral responses (e.g., changes to drug use or social networks), and a sense of collective responsibility to care for other people who use drugs ( , ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ). The Trauma-Informed Theory of Individual Health Behavior (TBB) adapts the United States Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration’s (SAMHSA) framework of Trauma-Informed Care (TIC) ( ) and explains the pathways from trauma to health behaviors ( ). SAMHSA outlines individual and sociocultural features that affect the experience and impact of trauma; emotional, physical, cognitive, behavioral, and existential reactions to trauma; and steps for organizations to implement TIC ( ). TBB posits that there are three forms of trauma that contribute to an individual’s trauma response: acute experiences of trauma, trauma-replicating environments, and historical trauma. The relationship between the trauma response and health behaviors are moderated by resilience factors ( i.e ., safety, autonomy, trauma awareness, trust). TBB is a novel theory that has not been yet applied to qualitative studies of substance use disorder (SUD) or overdose. This study adds to the qualitative literature of the experience of witnessing or responding to overdoses by focusing on trauma and applying TBB to an analysis of interviews with people who use drugs from multiple states in the US. The TTB model posits that the trauma response (e.g., the onset of PTSD symptoms) is most proximally shaped by the interaction between an acute experience of trauma, a trauma-replicating environment, and historical trauma. As this relates to overdose, we primarily focused on the interaction between individual factors that contributed to the overdose event and socio-ecological factors that tended to amplify the traumatic experience. These ranged from systemic gaps in services (such as the lack of resources to support overdose responders), harmful systems that created a more dangerous environment (e.g., policing), and more diffuse societal factors such as the stigma against people who use drugs that increased people’s sense of marginalization. While the TTB model also situates these within historical factors, we did not explicitly examine our subjects historically (as the study itself was cross-sectional). However, our analysis was informed by historically entrenched experiences of collective trauma against people who use drugs that may have contributed to a lack of engagement with paramedics or other resources. We interviewed individuals who have witnessed an overdose during the COVID-19 pandemic to understand the impact of these experiences on personal wellbeing and health behaviors. Our qualitative study offers insight into how

the stigma against people who use drugs that increased people’s sense of marginalization. While the TTB model also situates these within historical factors, we did not explicitly examine our subjects historically (as the study itself was cross-sectional). However, our analysis was informed by historically entrenched experiences of collective trauma against people who use drugs that may have contributed to a lack of engagement with paramedics or other resources. We interviewed individuals who have witnessed an overdose during the COVID-19 pandemic to understand the impact of these experiences on personal wellbeing and health behaviors. Our qualitative study offers insight into how people who witness overdoses experience the event, assign meaning to it, and how that meaning influences their behavior. Further, we explore whether witnessing overdoses was characterized as traumatic, whether repeated exposure resulted in cumulative trauma (conceptualized as a buildup of negative effects) or normalization (overdoses being accepted as “normal” or “natural”), and which coping mechanisms were used afterwards. Methods Participants were recruited from a larger parent study, the COVID Harm Reduction and Treatment Program Survey, which surveyed 570 people recruited from clients of 22 SUD treatment and harm reduction programs across nine states and Washington, DC, described elsewhere ( ; ). Data presented here are from a third data collection period which focused on in-depth interviews with overdose survivors and witnesses of overdose among the original sample of SUD treatment and harm reduction clients. We conducted hour-long semi-structured, in-depth phone interviews with 30 people who had experienced a personal overdose and/or witnessed at least one overdose during the COVID-19 pandemic. This article focuses on the participants who had witnessed overdoses ( N = 17). Before the interview, study team members obtained informed consent by phone. Participants were assigned unique study ID numbers to preserve anonymity. Participants received a $50 Visa gift card as remuneration. The interview guide was informed by the DSM-V screening checklist for PTSD ( ) and constructs of normalization of traumatic experiences ( ; ). As previous work described normalization of traumatic experiences among survivors of sexual violence and war veterans ( ; ), we asked about normalization of witnessing overdose. We also probed on DSM-V symptoms of PTSD ( ). The interview guide elicited participants’ narratives of overdoses they witnessed and included the following domains: witnessing and responding to overdose; social support afterwards; impact on mental health; and positives of witnessing. Although the eligibility criterion was witnessing an overdose during the COVID-19 pandemic, the interviews probed on multiple stories from participants who had witnessed multiple overdoses, including those before the pandemic. Interviews were audio recorded and transcribed. Research team members trained in trauma-informed interviewing (MS, ID, AM, HS, SH) conducted the interviews. Thematic content analysis (TCA) ( ) was conducted using ATLAS.ti ( ). TCA is a process in which inductive codes are created from common themes identified in the data and iteratively revised during the coding process. Themes are concepts that arise multiple times within and across transcripts; cases that contradict identified themes are discussed in the process of defining and naming themes and creating subthemes. TCA has been used in previous qualitative studies of overdose ( ; ). Team members open coded early transcripts separately, reviewed each other’s open coding, and met to discuss code construction. A codebook was developed from emerging themes from interviews, informed by the interview guide. The team met weekly throughout the interview and coding processes to discuss emerging themes from the interviews, revise the codebook, create and collapse subcodes, and regroup similar and dissimilar excerpts in an iterative process. Four out of 17 transcripts were double coded by the coding team (MS, ID, AM, HS) to refine and reach an agreed-upon coding framework. All transcripts were reviewed by the study team lead (SH) for consistency of code applications. As TBB expands beyond a list of PTSD symptoms by showing explanatory pathways between trauma and behavior, we used TBB to interpret the results in this manuscript to study how trauma from witnessing overdose and the trauma-replicating environment of drug use with others affect subsequent protective and risk behaviors. Study procedures were approved by the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health Institutional Review Board. To preserve anonymity and give context, we attribute participants’ quotes by stating their age, gender, and state of residence. Descriptions of the overdose event Participants described the setting and context of the overdose(s) they witnessed and what role they played in responding to the event. Some gave an account of the steps they took to respond to an overdose and reported that they did not feel panicked or scared because they knew what to do: “You just try to do what you got to do to bring them back, knock them out, Narcan, whatever, start CPR. And I know with me, during a messed up situation, I’m not thinking. I’m just trying to do what I got to do.” – 36-year-old man, NJ. However, many described feeling scared and panicked during the response and relieved when the person was revived: “I was petrified until I saw that he was starting to come to.” –50-year-old woman, NJ. Fatal overdoses elicited strong emotional reactions during the event and sometimes, in the retelling of the event. For example, one participant started to cry, when recounting the story of trying to revive someone who still died of the overdose. Factors contributing to degree of trauma Of the 15 participants who reportedly experienced trauma while witnessing an overdose, certain overdoses were described as more traumatic depending on the nature of the relationship, location, experience (or lack thereof) with overdose response, level of responsibility, outcome of the overdose, and frequency of overdose events. One participant who had talked about witnessing two separate overdose events—his fiancé and his fiancé’s friend—when asked about how he would feel if he witnessed another overdose, said: “If it’s somebody you care about, it’s always going to mess your head up. You don’t want nobody dying. I guess it’d be more comfortable and calm if it was somebody you didn’t know or didn’t care about too much. If it’s a loved one, somebody you care about, it should shake you up if you have any type of conscience or heart. I know it would with me.” – 36-year-old man, NJ For some, the personal nature of the overdose location was significant ( e.g ., someone overdosed at the participant’s house) because of the threat of consequences like eviction or because the location served as a reminder of the event and caused flashbacks. The sense of trauma was also amplified if they were the only one there to respond to it, or if it was their first time attempting to reverse an overdose: “This one was personal, this one was with me. This one was getting high with me. And this one, I had to do it myself, so it was different. Other times that I witnessed people overdose, I always either see the ambulance giving them Narcan or somebody from the streets giving them Narcan. But this one was close to me. This one was real scary.” – 48-year-old woman, PA. Others also expressed a distinction between witnessing and responding to overdoses, saying they were impacted more when they were the ones attempting to revive than when they watched others revive someone. Repeated experiences with little time to process them seemed to result in cumulative burden for participants. Some talked about the cumulative grief and trauma of seeing and responding to multiple overdoses. One of these participants was the default person everyone called upon for overdose response while she lived at a place where drugs were sold (referred to as a “trap house”). She reported that she had unintentionally assumed this role because she had amassed a “plethora” of naloxone from getting naloxone every time she went to a harm reduction organization. This was at a time when the organization required appointments (as a COVID-19 prevention measure) to access services, which may have posed a barrier for some. She described being overwhelmed by the psychological distress of repeatedly responding to overdose events: “Really, it doesn’t get less scary, I guess. Every time I have to do that, it takes it out of you. I mean, you’re the only thing keeping a human on this planet. I mean, what if you fail? Effects of trauma Many participants described symptoms of trauma in the aftermath, including physical, emotional, cognitive, and existential responses. Physical responses included trouble sleeping, nightmares, and physical manifestations of pain. One participant who saw her husband die of overdose reported chest pains. Participants reported emotional reactions after the event. Participants described feeling grief from losing friends and family to fatal overdoses. Participants reported feeling guilt and regret around contributing to the overdose (e.g., by giving that person drugs) or failing to do enough ( e.g ., by not noticing someone’s relapse or being unable to reverse the overdose). These feelings of guilt and regret are indicative of survivor guilt, a common experience following traumatic events ( ). Participants reported various cognitive reactions. Some reported they had “purposefully blocked out” and were avoiding processing the event(s). Others said that although they were calm or focused while responding to the overdose, they then found themselves ruminating on the experience afterwards or having flashbacks. Similarly, some described prospective anxiety about possibly not being able to save people in the future or in a hypothetical scenario. Four worried they would panic and not know what to do, even those who had naloxone training: “It is a very scary thought, though. At the moment, I have thoughts often about if something like that happened. And yes, I have it (naloxone) and I know what to do. But what if I froze? What if I panic and froze at the time? You don’t know what kind of a mental state you’re going to be in at that moment when anything could happen.” – 50-year-old woman, NJ. Participants experienced stress or fear thinking about failing to “save” someone as a “what if” to both past and future events. A few reported that they consequently made behavioral changes to protect themselves from further trauma or legal consequences, described in the section “ ” below. The primary existential reaction participants reported was normalization of witnessing overdoses. Many either implied or explicitly said that witnessing overdoses had become normalized, as they are “commonplace” in their lives and in certain areas of town that they see “one or two, maybe more than two every day.” For some, they described “muscle memory” they could rely on even if they were stressed while responding to an overdose. For others, knowing what to do after many experiences made them calmer and more focused on the response. Seeing, hearing about, and responding to overdoses was described by some as “just part of everything,” or an accepted risk: “It just kind of comes along with doing heroin” – 30-year-old woman, TN. Given the frequency of overdoses in participants’ lives, these quotes illustrate how participants have reworked their worldview to integrate witnessing and responding to overdoses into their expectation of drug use experiences and environments. However, many who endorsed normalization also described these events as traumatic, showing that normalization is not necessarily a protective factor against trauma. One participant even comforted her friend who was embarrassed that she overdosed: “It’s not that big a deal. Everybody at some point is going to OD, so just stop it” – 40-year-old woman, TN. Several remarked that many people who overdose do not see it as a reason to change their drug use behaviors; participants reported that some bystanders sought out the batch of drugs that caused someone’s overdose because it was a sign of potency, rather than avoid it due to risk of overdose. This could be interpreted as participants’ perception of normalization of overdose in other people who use drugs. However, some pushed back on the idea of seeing overdoses being “normal”: “I’m not going to say it’s normal, but it’s common. And when something is common, it really doesn’t have that type of mental effect on you. It’s sort of like you have become accustomed to it. So for me to talk about it, it doesn’t traumatize me” – 48-year-old man, PA. Some lamented that overdoses are so common in certain areas that people walk by individuals who are overdosing without looking or helping, showing “indifference” because they were “desensitized” to seeing overdoses. Coping resources Some participants showed religiosity, thanking God that they were able to reverse the overdose, that they were at the right place at the right time, or hoping that God would keep them from catching COVID-19 or other communicable diseases while they were giving rescue breaths to a stranger during the pandemic: “[My fiancé] was like, ‘Why would you do that? You have no idea if that person is sick or not.’ And I’m like, ‘You’re right, I don’t. But I’m not going to let them die because I don’t know that.’…And even before the pandemic, you don’t know what that person’s got. People who use needles carry around a lot of bad stuff and you never know. I got to figure if there’s some higher power out there, God or whatever, I would hope that if I’m trying to keep someone alive, He would keep me alive.” – 40-year-old woman, TN. Nearly half of participants reported feelings of heroism and self-efficacy after successfully saving someone from a fatal overdose: “I feel like it went better than it could have. I feel like I saved the day” – 41-year-old man, NY. Others reported increased feelings of self-efficacy for responding to overdoses in the future due to having naloxone and/or experience. One participant spread the knowledge he had gained from naloxone trainings to others on how to administer naloxone the correct way and another reported that she used the aftermath of responding to an overdose event as a teaching moment: “Every time I do help someone or give someone Narcan, I teach them how to use it. And I just hope they never have to use it on me ” – 40-year-old woman, TN. These quotes illustrate ways that participants recognized their impact and assigned meaning to the experience. Social support was consistently important as participants processed the event afterwards. On one hand, some described being a source of support for others. One example of this included the need to manage their feelings in order to support people around them to the detriment of their own coping: one participant pondered, “I can’t go through the emotions that I need to go through because of my kids…so when do I really have time to feel my feelings?” – 45-year-old woman, NJ. Others became closer with the person who had overdosed, and encouraged them to seek mental health and SUD treatment: “Just because he’s been using for such a long time, there’s always something wrong with us, like depression or something from using. So I just told him that he just needed to get some help like that, and it’s nothing to be embarrassed about. But he’s doing good now.” – 36-year-old woman, NJ. On the other hand, participants sought to receive social support from others. Some people talked to the people who were there at the same scene of the overdose, while others got support from people outside of the overdose experience, such as counselors, partners, friends, and family. One person recalled speaking to a harm reduction outreach worker: “He told me I did good (by reviving the person), and he supported me on the decisions that I made and what I had to do and I did. And he’s like, ‘That’s wonderful. I’m sorry that it happened, but I’m glad that you were there, and you knew what to do.’” – 49-year-old man, MI. Participants who had been using with the person who overdosed reported that they had a small circle of trusted people who were aware of their drug use that they could talk to. Behavioral responses After witnessing an overdose, some reported making or thinking about making changes to their social environment to protect themselves from witnessing another. Their motives were diverse and included the desire to avoid further trauma, guilt, liability, and legal repercussions. The participant mentioned above who was the “unofficial overdose responder” at a trap house eventually left due to the emotional toll of those experiences. Participants said that they were more likely to engage in solitary drug use to avoid having a drug use partner overdose: “I’m going to probably tend to try to not hang around people when I’m using and they’re using who are prone to have an overdose. It’s too much of a risk. It’s too much of everything…I think you feel almost partially responsible if they do that (overdose). What if I need to go and then all of a sudden they die?…God knows that shit is tough.” – 41-year-old man, NY. Some reported increased drug or alcohol use after witnessing an overdose. For example, one participant said, “Saving her is something that was going to give me nightmares, but that’s one of the main reasons why I use is to be numb, is not have to feel or think about the past or fucked up experiences.” – 36-year-old man, NJ. One of these participants described feelings of suicidality and nihilism underlying his increased drug use after he witnessed his best friend overdose: “It was almost like I was on a mission to join him… It was like if everything I love and my whole life can be upended that quickly, if something that important can be taken away just like that, I think I was like, ‘Well, what’s the point?’” – 46-year-old man, NJ. These behavioral responses of solitary drug use and increased use can contribute to increased personal overdose risk. Participants also reported making changes to reduce their personal overdose risk by making changes to their drug use or receiving treatment. Several made changes to their drug use and harm reduction behaviors (such as doing less, not using “back-to-back,” buying from a trusted source, and letting others use first to see the potency of the drugs, carrying naloxone). Others reported that they thought seriously about changing their drug use behaviors or going into treatment: one said that seeing the overdose made him “slow way down,” adding that, “I’ve been thinking about rehabbing it and trying to get done with it so that I can live a normal life and a happy life. But it’s just really hard.” – 49-year-old man, MI. Some people who identified as being in recovery expressed that their resolve to stay in recovery were strengthened after witnessing: “That’s what my older children was worried about. Me falling backwards, me going back. But like I said, that (husband dying of overdose) made me even stronger. You know what I’m saying? Because I don’t want to leave my children. I ain’t ready to go nowhere. My life to me is worth living, and I’m not trying to go nowhere.” – 45-year-old woman, NJ. Discussion In our study, participants said overdoses are commonplace in their lives, with factors such as degree of closeness to the person who overdosed making some overdose experiences more traumatic than others. Participants also expressed a range of responses to the overdose consistent with experiencing traumatic stress and grief, including guilt and prospective anxiety about witnessing another overdose. Previous studies have shown that a lack of access to effective coping strategies in response to these experiences can lead to self-medicating drug use and greater solitary drug use, which may place them at increased risk of overdose themselves ( ; ; ). Yet participants also described coping resources that helped to process the event including increased feelings of self-efficacy and social support in the aftermath. To our knowledge, this is the first study to apply TBB to a qualitative examination of trauma of witnessing and responding to overdoses among people who use drugs. We grounded our analyses in TBB and explored how the acute experiences of trauma, trauma-replicating environments, and historical trauma (i.e., historical and continued criminalization and stigmatization of drug use) affect health behaviors; and how that relationship is moderated by resilience factors (i.e., safety, autonomy, trauma awareness, and trust). Because people who use drugs are often the first to respond to overdoses ahead of or instead of emergency personnel ( ; ), and given that many people who use drugs prefer to be revived by a person with lived experience over professionals without lived experience ( ), it is paramount to understand the mental health impacts of witnessing and responding to overdoses for this population. Many reported that they witnessed multiple overdoses in their lifetime, which could be due to the trauma-replicating environment of a social network of people who use drugs. While there is some literature on how repeated traumatic events are processed among populations such as war veterans, survivors of sexual violence, and homeless mothers ( ; ; ), few studies have studied the psychological impacts of repeatedly witnessing overdoses ( ; ; ). As there is high overlap between individuals’ substance use networks and their social support networks ( ), there is a high likelihood of losing multiple close relations for many people who use drugs. Cumulative overdose events are associated with more severe responses of grief among people who use drugs ( ), as they may not have enough time to process one loss before the next happens, and they may be losing people from their social support and community ( ; ). In addition, bereaved people with SUD are more likely to have severe grief responses than those without SUD ( ), and people grieving overdose losses are more likely to meet symptom severity thresholds for PTSD and major depressive disorder than those grieving other sudden losses ( ). As the overdose crisis continues, the number of people suffering multiple overdose losses may be mounting. Our paper suggests that there is a subgroup of lay responders who are responding to overdoses on a regular basis. They could be more effectively identified by social services and harm reduction organizations and engaged in counseling and support, as these individuals are likely bearing a disproportionate emotional burden of caring for multiple people. Addressing the trauma-replicating environment of drug use with others is a complicated public health situation because naloxone distribution and training programs rely on others to be present at the time of an overdose. Previous studies, like ours, found a sense of communal responsibility among people who use drugs to help each other if someone overdoses ( , ; ). However, people who use drugs are also motivated to protect themselves from potential trauma or legal repercussions by avoiding people who frequently overdose or using alone ( ; ). In order to bolster the resilience factor of safety, it is necessary to improve awareness and implementation of Good Samaritan laws and repeal drug-induced homicide laws that are often used to prosecute bystanders at overdose events ( ; ; ). Continued expansion of naloxone distribution and education will increase the resilience factor of autonomy by increasing overdose response self-efficacy. The expansion of safe consumption sites and crisis stabilization centers could also help foster a safe but controlled environment to manage overdose outside of hospitals and off the streets, and take some of the burden off peer responders. Some reported that seeing overdoses had become normalized, although others resisted that characterization, and said that while common, it was not “normal” to them. Normalization is an existential response to trauma ( ), can reduce trauma awareness (one of the resilience factors of TBB), and with the compounding effect of stigmatization of drug use, decrease help-seeking behaviors. Repeated exposure to traumatic events can lead to cumulative trauma and/or normalization ( ). In our sample, a majority of participants (14 of 17) described the normalization of witnessing overdoses in their lives, yet many of those same participants reported feeling traumatized by either a specific event or the cumulative effect of witnessing many overdoses and losses. On one hand, normalization of overdose can be a helpful coping strategy to the extent that it helps people to confront a situation that may be common in their social environment. On the other hand, normalization of overdose may decrease help-seeking behaviors and harm reduction behaviors because witnessing overdose is no longer perceived as abnormal, severe, or signifying need of help ( ), and personal overdose becomes less threatening. A study on HIV-negative gay men who had lost countless friends to AIDS found normalization of death from AIDS and a decreased willingness to be vigilant about safer sex ( ). Statements such as “it just comes along with doing heroin” from our sample indicate normalization of overdose. Trauma-informed SUD care should include awareness of potential normalization of overdose. There is a need for mental health aftercare for people who use drugs who witness overdoses and lose loved ones to overdose. Some of this study’s participants reported getting social support after a witnessing event, but many did not. Aftercare could be modeled on programs similar to those for other professionals on the front lines of the opioid epidemic (e.g., paramedics, police officers) ( ; ). With increased awareness of the traumatic nature of witnessing overdoses, mental health aftercare could be integrated into encounters with harm reduction organizations during naloxone distribution, primary care settings, emergency department encounters, and SUD treatment providers. Personnel on the scene of an overdose could also be a source of help: for example, when outreach workers respond to an overdose, they could be purposeful in engaging with others who may have been at the scene. Peer-based support groups should routinely create space for discussions of grief to combat social withdrawal that can occur due to stigma and moral judgment around overdose deaths ( ; ). There is also a need to reduce barriers to mental health care and grief support in general and increase trust in healthcare providers for people who use drugs who are disproportionately affected by mental health issues and loss ( ). Previous research with people who use drugs has linked witnessing overdoses with PTSD ( ) and found instances of increased risk behaviors after witnessing overdoses, as well as increased protective behaviors ( ). Such risk behaviors found in our sample included increased drug use (to numb traumatic effects) and more isolated drug use (to self-protect from seeing another overdose), which may increase their personal overdose risk. Our study also found that some participants had increased motivation to change their drug use behaviors and start treatment after witnessing an overdose, which is in line with previous studies. A Vancouver study found that witnessing an overdose was associated with using drug checking services ( ). Another study found that following witnessing an overdose, the person who witnessed reported increased perceived importance of treatment both for people not in treatment and people receiving medications for opioid use disorder (MOUD) ( ). This aligns with our findings that participants reported increased interest in treatment after witnessing an overdose, and people in recovery expressed that their motivation to stay in recovery were strengthened after witnessing an overdose. Traumatic experiences can be leveraged to empower behavior change ( e.g ., reducing risky behaviors or stopping drug use, engaging in treatment, strengthening resolve to continue sobriety). By applying TBB to understand the pathways between witnessing overdose to health behaviors, we can better understand the effect of historical trauma (e.g., criminalization of drug use), trauma-replicating environments ( e.g ., social network of people who use drugs), and resilience factors ( e.g ., safety through Good Samaritan laws, autonomy through naloxone self-efficacy, trauma awareness through counseling, and trust in healthcare providers) and adapt interventions aimed at each construct of TBB. As social support was a significant theme in this study as in previous studies, we suggest that it is added as a resilience factor to TBB. This study had limitations. As social support was a significant theme in this study as in previous studies, we suggest that it is added as a resilience factor to TBB. This study had limitations. Foremost, it relied on people to reconstruct a traumatic event, and there may be gaps in recall and difficulty identifying a chronology and the associated experience. This is especially true because for some participants several months had elapsed since they had responded to an overdose. While a strength of the study was the geographic range (six states and Washington, DC) and varied demographics, it was not intended to be a representative sample. Participants were recruited from a larger parent study that included participants who engaged with treatment or harm reduction services. Thus, results may not be generalizable to the experiences of all people who use drugs. The traumatic nature of witnessing overdoses presents an opportunity to understand what people go through when they respond to an overdose. Trauma-informed approaches and grief literacy should be central for service providers and harm reduction organizations when they approach this subject with clients, and they should be aware of the effect of normalization on help-seeking behaviors. Importantly, increased motivation for behavior change after witnessing an overdose points to a window of opportunity for intervention.

1 Introduction Mental health is a state of well-being for every human being and essential for full development in all areas of life. The WHO indicates that it influences our actions and functions as an undeniable condition for every human being, as important as our physical health; essential for relating positively, contributing, building, obtaining a sense of satisfaction, and empathizing with people. However, in its absence, the individual may present obvious negative psychological and physical symptoms and even the appearance of serious medical conditions such as post-traumatic stress disorder, sleep disorders, cardiovascular diseases, and anxiety disorders ( ). The WHO (2022) relates the state of mental health to skills, habits, and emotions generated by the exchange of experiences with other people, so if you have poor mental health, it may be the product of the influence of psychological and physical factors. There are various internal and external factors that disturb its balance and give rise to a series of disorders that negatively impact the well-being of people. One of the most common and prevalent disorders today is anxiety, which has become a global public health problem, significantly affecting the quality of life of those who suffer from it WHO. Its main characteristic consists of a disproportionate alert response to situations perceived as threatening, generating a variety of psychological and physical symptoms, such as excessive worry, irritability, restlessness, and agitation ( ). Early and accurate identification of anxiety is crucial to initiate timely therapeutic interventions and prevent long-term complications, such as cardiovascular diseases and even suicide ( ). The research results demonstrate a broad panorama of diverse studies carried out worldwide. For example, ( ) identified a considerable increase in medical incidents related to mental health, in addition to finding 46 studies for depressive disorders and 29 related to anxiety disorders globally. These results led to the work of other researchers in the area focusing on anxiety disorders. In this sense, ( ), with reference to ( ), explains that there is a correlation between anxiety disorders and the emotional intelligence of the individual; and underlines a higher level of anxiety in women because they express, to a greater extent, their emotions regarding situations in their context. On the other hand, anxiety is considered a state of alert caused by situations that generate fear and excessive worry at any time in life, and they are of a psychological nature ( ). This defensive response, although useful in some cases, can cause a series of uncomfortable emotions: restlessness, irritability, hypervigilance, agitation, worry, among others. The findings of ( ) recorded a significant increase in cases of depression and anxiety. These disorders, especially anxiety, can manifest themselves in various ways, from mild restlessness to a state of constant alertness, as described by ( ). In the Mexican context, all federal entities have their own Health Law, however, ( ) reports on 14 federal entities in the national territory that have a Mental Health Law, representing 43.8%, and only five states define mental health within their Health Laws. Veracruz stands out for comparing the term mental health with the optimal state of complete mental, social, and emotional well-being. The actions to implement strengthening services in Mental Health for citizens correspond to the functions of the National Mental Health Council that has been operating since 2004. This body helps coordinate treatment policies. However, the unique context of everyone, such as the scarcity of economic resources, the level of education, even the stereotypes of society, among other factors, add complexity to receive adequate care. The selected studies show that, in Mexico, through the application of tests to identify anxiety disorders, ( ) they found a higher percentage of people with 58.89% in the Beck Depression and Anxiety Inventory test and 37.5% with the BAI test ( ). 11.10% of men in contrast to 25.3% of women in the same study were classified with severe anxiety during the confinement stage caused by COVID-19, so the methods used were aligned with the health regulations and must currently be applied again to evaluate in the post-covid stage. This systematic review aimed to provide a comprehensive analysis of Artificial Intelligence (AI) techniques and methodologies applied to anxiety disorder detection, focusing on their accuracy and research scope, in response to our core research questions: RQ1 (What Artificial Intelligence techniques show the best performance in identifying anxiety disorders in diverse populations?) and RQ2 (What methodologies and approaches have been adopted to train and validate Artificial Intelligence techniques in identifying anxiety disorders?). Regarding RQ1, the findings indicate a prevalent application of both Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) techniques across the analyzed studies, as highlighted in , . Deep Learning, in particular, demonstrated a more efficient performance in handling unstructured and multimodal data, and was used more frequently due to its broad range of applications and high algorithm accuracy. For instance, studies in China (2020) and Slovakia (2023) using DL showed high accuracies, such as 87% for anxiety detection and 87.88% for arousal classification from physiological signals, respectively. ML algorithms also proved effective, especially in brain image and text analysis, achieving accuracies of 90% in detecting neurocognitive abnormalities. These AI-driven methods generally exhibited higher accuracy compared to traditional anxiety disorder detection tests, offering valuable insights for improved diagnostic tools. In response to RQ2, a diversity of methodologies and approaches were adopted for training and validating these AI techniques. Studies utilized varied data sources, including self-reports, physiological data (e.g., heart rate, galvanic skin response, neuroimaging like fMRI, EEG), voice data, text data (from social media, questionnaires), and behavioral data. Validation methods typically involved cross-validation, independent datasets, and training-test divisions to evaluate algorithm effectiveness and consistency over time. Comparisons with traditional diagnostic methods were frequently observed, demonstrating the superiority of AI techniques in terms of diagnostic accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity. Specific algorithms identified included LSTM, Q-Learning, CNN-LSTM-CNN, SVM, Naive Bayes, Decision Tree, Random Forest, and Deep Neural Networks, reflecting a broad spectrum of AI applications. However, despite these promising advances, it is crucial to recognize that scientific research in this area is still in an early stage of development, at least in Mexico, and faces several significant challenges that limit its broader implementation and generalization. These challenges not only reside in the application of AI, but also in the characteristics of the data and the methodologies employed in the existing studies. It should be noted that a large part of the filtered studies focused on samples that were often small and homogeneous, raising significant questions about the generalizability of the results to more diverse populations in real clinical practice.
