In response, this integrative review aims to comprehensively examine the barriers and facilitators influencing the transition from oncology to palliative care for advanced cancer patients within the context of healthcare services. Through synthesising existing research, this review seeks to provide insights for enhancing the transition process and improving patient outcomes within healthcare service settings. Design Literature review approach The integrative review was performed to analyse recent evidence involving both experimental and non-experimental research to gain a comprehensive understanding of the topic [ ]. A systematic approach was carried out to ensure replicability and transparency [ ]. Population/Patient, Exposure and Outcome (PEO) format was used to formulate a research review question [ ]. In line with this approach, the research question addressed in this review is: What are the barriers and facilitators in the process of transition from oncology to palliative care of adult people with advanced cancer? Search strategy A systematised comprehensive search was conducted across four databases: PubMed, PsycINFO, CINAHL and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) using MeSH and text words and respected Boolean logic (Table ). MeSH terms “children”, “adolescent” and “paediatrics” were added with a NOT Boolean operator. Hand-searching of reference lists and forward citation tracking were also performed for included studies. The search was limited to articles published in English from 2010 to 2023 to reflect the current practices and trends. The search was executed between March and May 2023. Selection of articles B.G. and T.R. employed Rayyan software for systematic article eligibility assessments [ ], ensuring unbiased blind reviews of titles and abstracts based on specified criteria (Table ). This approach aimed to enhance overall efficiency and maintain objectivity throughout the evaluation process. In instances of disagreements, resolutions were reached through discussions involving B.G., T.R., M.A., and E.G. Subsequently, a comprehensive assessment of the full texts was conducted. Figure presents a PRISMA flowchart of the search strategy. Data extraction and analysis A predefined extraction sheet systematically gathered data from included articles, aligning with the operational definition of the transition concept [ ]. The focus was on barriers and facilitators in the transition from oncology to palliative care, covering goals of care, care settings and management. Data matrices were developed to facilitate the systematic organisation of the extracted data, offering a comprehensive overview of each included article (Annex ). Following a four-step process in line with integrative review methods, an inductive thematic analysis identified key themes through data familiarisation, initial code generation, organisation into groups and final theme identification [ ]. Results Out of 180 articles screened, 38 met the inclusion criteria. The results are presented in two sections: the first summarises the included studies, while the second delineates identified barriers and facilitators across six key categories. Overview of included studies Reviewed articles spanned 13 countries, including two multinational studies. The majority were from the United States ( n = 14), followed by Australia ( n = 3), Canada ( n = 3), the United Kingdom ( n = 2), Belgium ( n = 2) and Japan ( n = 2). Individual articles were reported from Brazil, China, France, Italy, Norway, Taiwan and Uganda. Fourteen studies were quantitative, twenty were qualitative and four employed mixed methods. Data collection included interviews in twenty-two studies, focus groups in four and surveys in eleven. Thirty-one studies included the perspective of medical professionals, two studies focused on family members’ views, four explored patients’ experiences and eight analysed patients’ electronic medical health records. Further details in Annex and Annex summarise the results. Barriers and facilitators to transition Knowledge and understanding about disease trajectory and palliative care Patients and families Knowledge and health literacy play a crucial role in patients’, families’ and healthcare professionals’ approach towards palliative care transition. Numerous studies emphasised the critical role of the terminology used, particularly the term “palliative care”. Specifically, many patients associated “hospice” with imminent death and, due to confusion between “hospice” and “palliative care,” perceived palliative care as exclusively related to terminal care and dying [ – ]. Using softer terminology, such as “supportive care”, was reported to be advantageous when discussing the referral, with patients being more receptive to it, making it easier for them to develop strategies for the transition [ , , , ]. Poor communication around disease progression and treatment intent was recognised as another barrier [ ]. Patients and their families may hesitate to engage in conversations about end-of-life and palliative care, often due to perceived denial and resistance to acceptance [ , ]. Thirteen studies noted that patients’ reluctance to accept their prognosis and engage in palliative care discussions can be attributed to a limited understanding of their disease trajectory, potentially leading to denial

when discussing the referral, with patients being more receptive to it, making it easier for them to develop strategies for the transition [ , , , ]. Poor communication around disease progression and treatment intent was recognised as another barrier [ ]. Patients and their families may hesitate to engage in conversations about end-of-life and palliative care, often due to perceived denial and resistance to acceptance [ , ]. Thirteen studies noted that patients’ reluctance to accept their prognosis and engage in palliative care discussions can be attributed to a limited understanding of their disease trajectory, potentially leading to denial of palliative care referrals [ , , , , – ]. Patients struggling with acceptance and understanding of their prognosis may find it difficult to accept the need for the early introduction of palliative care [ ]. Some individuals exhibit hesitancy towards palliative care because they are still receiving ongoing treatment, and even if proven ineffective, they hold on to hope for a potential cure [ , ]. Thus, the importance of health literacy of patients and families becomes particularly evident when addressing the transition to palliative care [ ]. The receptiveness to palliative care referrals can vary among patients, with some being more open while others resist until the late stages of the disease [ ]. Hence, paying close attention to patients’ cues, adopting a holistic approach and engaging in open communication about the disease prognosis are essential [ , , ]. Introducing palliative care in the early stages and presenting it as a welcoming and highly skilled resource can be beneficial in dispelling misconceptions and averting potential negative emotional responses [ , ]. Likewise, an additional facilitator for palliative care referrals is the early recognition of the need for conversations about end-of-life considerations, goals of care, treatment expectations, and the skilful navigation of the balance between hope and reality during these discussions [ , ]. Nevertheless, a pervasive challenge in palliative care is the prevalence of communication difficulties with patients and their families often rooted in a lack of training in essential communication skills, resulting in the complexities of delivering sensitive information and effectively managing the emotional toll [ – , , , , , , – ]. Research involving oncologists from diverse specialities revealed that the existing societal stigmas associated with the topic of dying could make end-of-life discussions challenging for some physicians caring for patients with advanced cancer [ ]. Therefore, implementing emotional management training and strategies for emotional detachment can prevent burnout and compassion fatigue when navigating discussions about distressing news [ ]. Healthcare professionals Healthcare professionals’ understanding and knowledge about palliative care may cause a wide array of misconceptions and misunderstandings [ , , , , , , , , , ]. A study in Canada showed that the specialisation of referring oncologists affected the early referral to specialised palliative care services, with medical oncologists referring less frequently than surgical or radiation oncologists [ ]. Moreover, oncologists who treat patients with solid tumours may see palliative care as a valuable source of expertise that can help alleviate the burden on cancer clinics, albeit haematologists, who might lack training and expertise in palliative care referrals, might perceive palliative care as incompatible with cancer care, only referring to it when curative treatment options have been exhausted [ , ]. Additionally, some clinicians may lack an understanding of the multidisciplinary approach, the role of palliative care, and when to introduce these services, possibly due to limited knowledge or stigmas associated with them [ , , , ]. Cultural aspects and underlying assumptions The majority of studies included in the review identified barriers and facilitators considering cultural aspects. A language barrier emerged as a common obstacle when transitioning from oncology to palliative care [ , , ]. A study in the United States reported that physicians without a shared language with patients relied on interpreters for accurate communication and needed to trust their ability to accurately convey messages [ ]. Correspondingly, being a member of an ethnic minority and having conflicting cultural norms and religious beliefs can also affect the fluency of the referral process, as in some cultures, openly discussing death may be seen as disrespectful or as causing a loss of hope [ , , , , – ]. Certain religious beliefs may conflict with recommended treatments, challenging health professionals to navigate ethical responses [ ]. In specific cultural contexts, exemplified in a Japanese study, people’s reluctance to welcome strangers, including healthcare professionals, into their homes acts as a barrier to introducing home-based palliative care [ ]. Also, first-generation migrants may rely on traditional views in medical interactions, whilst the more culturally exposed second-generation tends to align with mainstream perspectives in engaging with physicians [ ]. The involvement of the patient’s family in decision-making, coupled with

as causing a loss of hope [ , , , , – ]. Certain religious beliefs may conflict with recommended treatments, challenging health professionals to navigate ethical responses [ ]. In specific cultural contexts, exemplified in a Japanese study, people’s reluctance to welcome strangers, including healthcare professionals, into their homes acts as a barrier to introducing home-based palliative care [ ]. Also, first-generation migrants may rely on traditional views in medical interactions, whilst the more culturally exposed second-generation tends to align with mainstream perspectives in engaging with physicians [ ]. The involvement of the patient’s family in decision-making, coupled with potential resistance to disclosing distressing information to shield patients from suffering and maintain a positive atmosphere, poses another barrier to a smooth transition [ , , ]. Additionally, a study in Australia revealed that having families with limited capacity to support a patient may be a facilitator of a palliative care transition [ ]. Age adds complexity to transitioning from oncology to palliative care. Particularly for younger patients with haematological malignancies who still hold hope for curative treatment, which can serve as a potential barrier to referral [ ]. Interestingly, conflicting results with young age were found across studies with several identifying it as a barrier [ , , , , ]; while in others, it was seen as a facilitator [ , , ]. Moreover, being female [ , , , ] and belonging to the White and Asian race [ ] were noted as facilitators, while being of a non-white race acted as a barrier to an early referral [ ]. Other demographic factors such as lower education levels appeared as facilitators in an Italian study [ ], while being married or having a partner emerged as facilitators in a study conducted in Brazil [ ]. Demographic characteristics of physicians were identified as potential barriers - including the female gender of referring physicians [ ] and the older age of oncologists who may not be familiar with palliative care [ ], making them less likely to refer. Also, African-American physicians, compared to White-American physicians in the United States, were less likely to refer patients to hospice for psychosocial, religious and spiritual support [ ]. Shortcomings in economic coverage for services Eight studies included in the review identified barriers in relation to financial elements in transition in various regions of the world. Notably, additional costs associated with palliative care services and concerns regarding the eligibility of these services for insurance coverage were evident barriers [ , , ]. According to a study in the United States, concerns may be associated with insurance co-payments or reimbursement [ ]. In the Japanese context, long-term care insurance fails to cover nurses’ visits for patients with a higher degree of dependence, resulting in a more pronounced financial burden for younger cancer patients [ ]. According to two studies in the United States, some clinicians are concerned that referring to palliative care could prolong hospital stays and increase utilisation rates [ , ]. In addition, in Belgium and Taiwan, a lack of resources to support early palliative care involvement was highlighted as an apparent challenge [ , ]. Furthermore, an Australian study and a study conducted in various European countries reported that the lack of resources for palliative care within their respective institutions negatively affected the number of referrals to palliative care services as did the absence of financial structures to support this purpose [ , ]. Besides, the lack of financial incentives for community care physicians was a factor that could potentially reduce patient referrals [ ]. Characteristics of the patient clinical situation Multiple studies have reported that predicting palliative care needs is more challenging for haematological malignancies when compared to solid malignancies [ , , , , ]. Furthermore, database records and surveys showed that individuals with lung cancer received fewer palliative care referrals in comparison to other solid cancer types, including urological cancers, upper and lower gastrointestinal cancers, gynaecological or breast cancers [ , , , , ]. Several studies noted that undergoing palliative chemotherapy, curative treatment, or participation in clinical trials could pose a potential barrier [ , , , ]. Moreover, the challenge of determining the optimal timing for introducing palliative care, particularly when the patient’s prognosis is difficult to estimate, was identified as another potential barrier [ , , ]. People with advanced cancer were more commonly referred to palliative care services when they had a decline in their health condition, high rates of metastatic disease, and higher comorbidity burden [ , , , ]. Furthermore, a positive response to the “surprise” question - “Would you be surprised if a patient died within 6 [ ] or 12 months [ ]? ”- served as a facilitator of a referral to specialist palliative care. Physicians displayed greater willingness to

introducing palliative care, particularly when the patient’s prognosis is difficult to estimate, was identified as another potential barrier [ , , ]. People with advanced cancer were more commonly referred to palliative care services when they had a decline in their health condition, high rates of metastatic disease, and higher comorbidity burden [ , , , ]. Furthermore, a positive response to the “surprise” question - “Would you be surprised if a patient died within 6 [ ] or 12 months [ ]? ”- served as a facilitator of a referral to specialist palliative care. Physicians displayed greater willingness to initiate end-of-life care when they perceived that the burden of comorbidity precluded the delivery of effective or potentially curative therapy and when disease-directed therapies were significantly worsening patients’ quality of life [ ]. Furthermore, frequent visits to an emergency department have been demonstrated to hinder the introduction of palliative care to people with advanced cancer [ ]. Relational dynamics between patients and professionals and among professionals A closer relationship developed between health professionals, including oncologists, nurses, general practitioners, palliative care specialists, cancer patients and family members during cancer treatment, was essential in initiating and managing patients’ transition from oncology to palliative care. Namely, over the course of their illness, many patients develop close emotional relationships with their physicians, which can be a barrier for physicians when initiating conversations about the end of life and referral to palliative care [ , , , , , , , ]. In particular, oncologists are concerned that patients and family members may perceive palliative care referral as abandonment, potentially impeding the transition process [ , ]. One study found that haematologists may also hesitate to refer patients with advanced cancer to palliative care services, being reluctant to “give up” on their patients even when the chances of a cure are minimal [ ]. In light of these challenges, establishing familiarity with health professionals closely involved with cancer patients becomes crucial for the transition process. Two studies highlighted that cultivating an open and honest relationship with patients may indeed enhance the transition to palliative care [ , ]. Nevertheless, these established emotional connections with patients also make it challenging for medical and nursing staff to hand patients over to new doctors in the palliative care approach [ ]. Additionally, frequent visits to the cancer centre may further hinder patients from forming connections with the palliative care team [ ]. Delayed referrals by oncologists, motivated by the desire to shield patients from emotional distress when meeting new healthcare providers in the advanced stages of illness, can also contribute to this issue [ ]. Furthermore, family members’ concerns about patients developing relationships with unfamiliar medical staff are significantly associated with perceived late palliative care referrals [ ]. Poor rapport and superficial communication among health professionals were found to inhibit palliative care transitions, while close and face-to-face relationships facilitated them [ , , , , , , , ]. Involving healthcare professionals in fostering active professional relationships within departments enhances smaller-scale collaborations, facilitating the transition of advanced cancer patients from hospital care to home-based palliative care [ ]. Moreover, nurturing a feedback culture and a collaborative approach to care among health professionals can strengthen cooperation and improve the care transition experience [ , ]. Although most oncologists agree that early referrals to palliative care benefit patients, some may restrain from initiating this transition due to potential care goals conflicts as they may not see palliative care service as compatible with active ongoing cancer treatments [ , ]. In addition, some oncologists have concerns that palliative care specialists could interfere with or discourage active oncological therapy [ ]. A sense of professional ownership and the need to have control over the treatment process often lead some oncologists to perceive the referral to palliative care as their own professional failure [ , ]. Likewise, some oncologists felt that the decision-making process relies exclusively on them and perceived a lack of support from the palliative care services [ ]. Notably, a sense of ownership of the treatment process was particularly emphasised in situations of having a prior negative experience with palliative care services [ , ]. The hierarchical nature of relationships among different health professionals can create barriers to the transition, as the referral to palliative care typically requires initiation and approval from oncologists [ ]. Viewing palliative care services as separate entities, rather than integral parts of their practice, can also hinder the transition [ ]. Organisational issues involving limitations and fragmentation of care The organisation and management of oncology departments and palliative care services play a crucial role in influencing the transition process. Excessive workload can lead to physical and emotional exhaustion in oncologists, making it challenging to manage patients’ transition [ ]. Resource constraints, including limitations in time

among different health professionals can create barriers to the transition, as the referral to palliative care typically requires initiation and approval from oncologists [ ]. Viewing palliative care services as separate entities, rather than integral parts of their practice, can also hinder the transition [ ]. Organisational issues involving limitations and fragmentation of care The organisation and management of oncology departments and palliative care services play a crucial role in influencing the transition process. Excessive workload can lead to physical and emotional exhaustion in oncologists, making it challenging to manage patients’ transition [ ]. Resource constraints, including limitations in time and space, can impede oncologists’ capacity to engage in open, honest end-of-life conversations and oversee coordination and transition planning for patients [ , , , ]. Furthermore, a lack of well-defined professional roles and responsibilities can cause confusion among healthcare professionals regarding the diverse facets of care provision, ultimately deterring the transition process [ ]. Lack of availability of services and health professionals has been recognised as essential barriers to transition, potentially leading to delays in palliative care referrals [ , , , , , ]. Issues related to the availability of appointments and timely access to palliative care may impede the early application of such care [ , ]. Also, the involvement of discharge nurses has been linked to a more streamlined transition process, underlining the significance of having adequate resources and healthcare professionals in place to facilitate the transition from oncology to palliative care [ ]. The place of residence can impact the transition process, with some studies identifying living in urban areas as a barrier [ , ], and others as a facilitator [ ]. Additionally, being a local patient referred from a cancer centre or residing close to palliative care services appeared to result in more frequent palliative care referrals [ , ]. Several studies found that having palliative care services in different locations or physically distant areas has a negative impact on the transition process [ , , , ], as patients often face travel-related challenges when accessing palliative care services [ ]. Moreover, disparities in the organisation of palliative care services across regions within a country, coupled with variations in the acknowledgement of palliative care subspecialties, can pose a challenge in navigating the transition process [ , ]. The heterogeneity of palliative care services also contributes to reluctance among home physicians to integrate palliative care into their practice [ , ]. Eight studies identified the absence of specific guidelines and protocols for referral as a barrier [ , , , , , , , ]. Addressing this challenge through the establishment of standardisation and support of coordination tools, including primary care reports, referral criteria, identifying patients’ needs, having tools for initiating advance care planning discussions holds the potential to increase the rates of palliative care referrals [ , , , , , ]. Complicated bureaucratic procedures and incomplete discharge paperwork are also acknowledged as obstacles in the transition process [ , ]. These challenges can be compounded by differences in patient assessment models and electronic medical records across services [ , ]. Improving the visibility of patients’ charts has been shown to enhance palliative care application in the treatment process [ ]. However, specialised palliative care admission criteria can limit some patients’ access to palliative care services [ ]. Furthermore, palliative care services which accept patients receiving chemotherapy have been shown to facilitate the transition [ ]. Despite this, the lack of general practitioners’ involvement in the transition process is also recognised as a barrier [ ]. To address such challenges, implementing a shared holistic model of care, embedding palliative care in oncology practices, and becoming familiar with palliative care services can improve early referrals and the transition process [ , ]. Finally, stakeholder involvement through implementing and funding new legislation may further increase patients’ enrolment in palliative care [ ]. Discussion In this integrative review of empirical studies, we explored the barriers and facilitators surrounding the transition from oncology to palliative care in adults with cancer. A significant finding of this review is the pervasive stigma associated with the terms “palliative care”, which can greatly influence the willingness of patients and their families to embrace the transition to palliative care. Encouraging the early integration of palliative care involves promoting alternative, patient-preferred terms that resonate better with patients. These include “supportive care”, “pain team”, “symptom management”, or “symptom control”, all of which carry more positive connotations [ – ]. The stigma in the context of early palliative care referral, is likely influenced by sociocultural and religious factors, as well as attitudes towards death acceptance [ , – ]. High health literacy facilitates understanding and contributes to informed choices and the successful completion of treatment options [ – ]. Moreover, this review showed that family

to embrace the transition to palliative care. Encouraging the early integration of palliative care involves promoting alternative, patient-preferred terms that resonate better with patients. These include “supportive care”, “pain team”, “symptom management”, or “symptom control”, all of which carry more positive connotations [ – ]. The stigma in the context of early palliative care referral, is likely influenced by sociocultural and religious factors, as well as attitudes towards death acceptance [ , – ]. High health literacy facilitates understanding and contributes to informed choices and the successful completion of treatment options [ – ]. Moreover, this review showed that family and informal caregivers play a crucial role in the transition to palliative care, serving as both barriers and facilitators. Their knowledge, receptiveness to terminology, communication dynamics, and emotional connections with healthcare professionals significantly influence the process. By actively involving caregivers in the decision-making process and providing them with adequate support and education, healthcare professionals may enhance the overall care experience for patients facing advanced illness, and their families. This review acknowledged that discussions about palliative care may be impeded by factors such as religion and culture, particularly cultural taboos linked to cancer and death. Notably, cultural and religious differences in end-of-life care, especially within Western countries dealing with minority populations, present challenges rooted in individual belief systems [ , ]. These challenges are compounded by the influence of specific religions on perceptions of palliative care, which in turn affects the healthcare system, highlighting the need to understand cultural constructs and preferences [ ]. This review also emphasises racial and ethnic disparities in the transition to palliative care, exposing how cultural aspects, including minority status, influence perspectives on illness and practices. Patients in culturally diverse populations often avoid discussing these matters to preserve hope, relying on religious faith as a major coping strategy, which hampers the transition to palliative care and the acceptance of the diagnosis and treatment [ ]. Therefore, physicians should respect the family’s social, cultural, or religious beliefs, particularly when low health literacy, limited education, or a disadvantaged socioeconomic status may play a role [ ]. Sensitivity is crucial when discussing palliative care, as some individuals may associate the term with negative connotations, viewing it as a euphemism for death [ , ] or interpreting it as giving up on patients [ – ]. Therefore, this review reported the importance of oncologists requiring specialised training to navigate sensitive topics effectively and engage patients in decision-making. The findings in this paper emphasise the importance of strong doctor–patient communication skills in palliative care, particularly within multidisciplinary teams. Although discussions about disease progression and treatment intent are typically initiated by treating oncologists, challenges in communicating aspects such as alignment with patients’ goals can persist across the care team, creating substantial barriers. Inadequate communication about disease progression and treatment intent serves as a substantial barrier, with patients’ limited understanding of their disease trajectory recognised as a universal challenge [ , ]. This lack of comprehension and poor communication, applicable beyond cancer patients to those managing chronic conditions [ ], highlights the common issue of ineffective communication in the transition to palliative care, compromising patient and caregiver autonomy in decisions about treatment or end-of-life preparations. Recognising patients’ core values fosters professional sensitivity to patients’ emotions, thoughts, and decisions, enabling them to communicate preferences and make decisions aligned with their perspectives on a fulfilling life, which is a particularly important process when dealing with adults facing incurable cancer [ , ]. This review demonstrated that establishing effective relationships between health professionals is essential for delivering advanced patient care across palliative care. Collaborative interactions and open communication across specialities contribute to a holistic and patient-centred approach, not only in palliative care but across the broader medical care spectrum [ ]. For instance, a study in Norway reported that regular, short intervals for sharing patient information have been identified as a factor that enhances local collaboration among rural health professionals in primary palliative care [ ]. Open and efficient communication not only enhances understanding but also underlines the importance of diplomacy in navigating healthcare practices and integrating palliative care across disciplines, thereby preserving its distinctive language and core values ultimately benefiting both professionals and patient outcomes [ , ]. In fields like oncology and palliative care, where the complexity of patient cases often requires a multidisciplinary approach, the importance of cohesive teamwork becomes even more apparent. Some oncologists view periods of complex symptoms or challenging clinical situations as appropriate moments to initiate palliative care referrals or collaboration, thereby facilitating cooperation [ ]. Tumour boards, which bring together specialists from various disciplines, illustrate how effective professional relationships can result in well-informed treatment plans tailored to individual patient needs [ ]. Similarly, within advanced medical care, characterised by complex treatments and decisions, a strong provider-patient relationship takes on

[ , ]. In fields like oncology and palliative care, where the complexity of patient cases often requires a multidisciplinary approach, the importance of cohesive teamwork becomes even more apparent. Some oncologists view periods of complex symptoms or challenging clinical situations as appropriate moments to initiate palliative care referrals or collaboration, thereby facilitating cooperation [ ]. Tumour boards, which bring together specialists from various disciplines, illustrate how effective professional relationships can result in well-informed treatment plans tailored to individual patient needs [ ]. Similarly, within advanced medical care, characterised by complex treatments and decisions, a strong provider-patient relationship takes on paramount importance. This review revealed that establishing trust is essential to palliative care transitions, as patients need confidence in their healthcare providers’ expertise and intentions. This trust lays the foundation for open communication, enabling patients to express concerns, preferences and uncertainties [ ]. Healthcare outcomes are especially influenced by resource availability, with adequate facilities, personnel, and technology being critical for effective and timely care. Regions with limited resources often experience delays in diagnosis, treatment, and access to essential medications, impacting overall patient health [ ]. Furthermore, inadequate referral guidelines and protocols emerged as a barrier in this review. Addressing this challenge through standardised coordination tools, holds promise for increasing referral rates and improving care transitions. The absence of specific guidelines fuels ongoing discussions about inappropriate treatment, raising questions about the optimal time for transitioning to palliative care and the prolongation of intense treatments. Timely access to palliative care within a mixed generalist-specialist model can reduce the likelihood of potentially inappropriate end-of-life care for cancer patients, emphasising the crucial role of generalist palliative care [ ]. Additionally, increasing digital opportunities for patient access to files and professional sharing of patient documentation can facilitate coordination and communication, addressing challenges associated with insufficient referral guidelines [ – ]. It is noteworthy that the reviewed articles did not explore e-health solutions. Strengths and limitations While integrative reviews may not offer the depth of systematic reviews, the inclusion of blind reviewing software added rigour and reduced bias in the selection process of included articles. This review primarily relies on perspectives from healthcare professionals, which may limit the scope of patient experiences. Nevertheless, it captures recent healthcare developments, providing valuable opportunities for future research aimed at improving the transition process for patients with advanced cancer. Moreover, examining diverse time frames may yield insights into the persistence or evolution of challenges in oncology and palliative care. Conclusion The review highlights critical factors influencing the transition to palliative care, including literacy in disease trajectories and palliative care, communication, cultural aspects, economic considerations, organisational issues, patient clinical characteristics, and the dynamics between patients and healthcare providers. Understanding these barriers and facilitators is essential for improving the palliative care transition process and ensuring optimal care for patients facing advanced cancer. Specialist training is necessary to equip healthcare providers with the skills needed to navigate these complex issues effectively. Moreover, adopting standardised coordination tools within hospital settings, such as integrating primary care reports, defining clear referral criteria, and systematically documenting patients’ needs, may significantly enhance the timeliness and quality of advance care planning discussions. A collaborative effort of healthcare professionals, policymakers, patients and healthcare organisations is imperative to devise strategies aimed at streamlining the transition to palliative care, thereby delivering comprehensive support to patients and their families. chunks.content: What is already known about the topic Palliative patients and informal carers often suffer from distressing symptoms and burden that can be alleviated through palliative psychological support and targeted group-specific interventions. What this paper adds Psychologists and psycho-oncologists in Germany most frequently use non-specific cross-school, low-threshold, needs- and resource-oriented psychological interventions. Practitioners are less familiar with life review techniques, meaning- and dignity-centred interventions, logotherapy and existential analysis methods, and systemic and hypnotherapeutic approaches. The use of psychological interventions is influenced by further training in palliative care for psychologists and professional experience (years working as a psychologist/psycho-oncologist in a palliative care setting). Implications for practice, theory or policy To make palliative psychological care truly evidence based and comparable, a comprehensive conceptual framework with practice guidelines is required. The development of a consensus-based taxonomy of suitable psychological/psychotherapeutic approaches and interventions for palliative care could greatly benefit educational institutions, stakeholders, and future research projects. Introduction Palliative patients suffer not only from physical symptoms but also from psychological, spiritual and social distress⁠ [ – ]. The psychological experiences of serious physical illness and approaching death can range from adequate emotional responses to psychiatric comorbidities and disorders. Psycho-existential distressing symptoms like anxiety, depression, hopelessness, demoralization, loss of meaning or dignity, discouragement, pointlessness, being trapped by the illness and even wishes to hasten death are common [ , – ]. Based on meta-analytical data, the combined prevalence of psychiatric syndromes (all types of depression, anxiety and adjustment disorders) in cancer patients and palliative care patients is reported to be 38.2% [ ]. Consequently, the German S3 guideline for palliative medicine recommends that, in the event of a mental disorder, guideline-compliant diagnosis and therapy with psychotherapeutic, psychiatric and/or pharmacological expertise should also be offered at the end of life [ ]. In a German cohort study existential distress (including demoralization, death anxiety and dignity-related distress) was described in 46.4% of patients with advanced cancer [ ]. Informal carers are also affected in many ways by witnessing the illness, feeling overburdened or exhausted by provision of ongoing support, worries, fears or anticipatory grief [ – ]. To accurately and comprehensively identify and treat the wide range of symptoms and experienced distress in accordance with guidelines, the integration of palliative psychology expertise into multiprofessional palliative care teams (MPCT) is essential and highly recommended [ , – ]. Often, this seems to be optional, subject to widely varying national and international regulations, and is therefore repeatedly described as inadequate [ – ]. Furthermore, there seem to be significant shortcomings in the competence of non-psychological health care professionals in recognising psychological distress and in providing or arranging adequate psychological support [ – ]. Psychologists and psychotherapists themselves also express a need for additional training for example in systemic therapy, dignity therapy, narrative therapy, life story work, acceptance and commitment therapy, and mindfulness-based stress reduction [ ]. Strada therefore suggests a very comprehensive skill set for palliative psychologists, which includes diagnostic, psychotherapeutic, psychiatric, pharmacological, palliative care, ethical-legal and cultural knowledge in dealing with the seriously ill, the dying and their relatives [ ]. In Germany, conventional psychotherapy is regulated by law, is provided by licensed psychotherapists and aims to treat mental disorders and restore mental and physical functioning using guideline-based diagnostic and manualised interventions [ ]. In contrast, psycho-oncological care addresses the complex, changing needs of cancer patients and is provided by physicians or academically trained psychosocial professionals (e.g., psychology or social pedagogy at master’s level qualifying for a scientifically recognised psychotherapeutic approach) who have completed certified additional psycho-oncological training [ ]. Palliative psychology, as a relatively new subdiscipline of psychology, focuses on the treatment and support of seriously ill and dying patients with all forms of life-limiting illnesses, as well as the support of their relatives [ ]. The steady development of this discipline in recent years was fostered by a basic curriculum [ ], further training in palliative care for psychologists [ ], the definition of a professional profile for psychologists in palliative care [ ], and the opportunity to become certified as a specialist palliative care psychologist [ ]. Scheiner et al. discuss the different qualification requirements and fields of activity of these psychological professions in greater detail [ ]. The actual nature of psychologists’ work in palliative care, as well as its integration, has not been systematically researched to date [ , , ]. Beyond classic psychological/psychotherapeutic intervention methods, specific interventions from the existential and humanistic approaches, such as life review procedures focusing on meaning and dignity, are described as being particularly effective and supportive in palliative care settings [ – ]. They unfold their positive effects for example by enhancing sense of dignity through narrative richness [ ]. Quality of life and psychospiritual well-being can be improved by strengthening sense of meaning and experiencing inner peace [

]. The actual nature of psychologists’ work in palliative care, as well as its integration, has not been systematically researched to date [ , , ]. Beyond classic psychological/psychotherapeutic intervention methods, specific interventions from the existential and humanistic approaches, such as life review procedures focusing on meaning and dignity, are described as being particularly effective and supportive in palliative care settings [ – ]. They unfold their positive effects for example by enhancing sense of dignity through narrative richness [ ]. Quality of life and psychospiritual well-being can be improved by strengthening sense of meaning and experiencing inner peace [ , ]. They may also enable life reassessment through remembrance and life review [ ]. Recommendations and evidence for palliative psychological support and care can be summarised into seven key aspects: (a) early integration of palliative psychological expertise to reliably assess and record the psychological and existential symptom burden experienced by patients and their relatives to derive appropriate support needs (e.g. exploration, diagnostics and screening) [ , , ]; (b) use of low-threshold, resource-oriented psychological interventions to support coping with illness and decision-making, and to promote self-efficacy (e.g. psychological counselling, ethical counselling, psychoeducation, resource collection, exploration and activation of coping strategies and impact techniques) [ , , ]; (c) use of psychological interventions to support the management of distressing physical symptoms, such as pain, nausea, breathlessness or weakness (e.g. mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR) interventions [ , ], hypnotherapy [ – ], body psychotherapy [ ], interventions from embodiment research [ ], relaxation techniques [ ] and guided imagery [ ]); (d) use of psychological and/or psychotherapeutic interventions which go beyond psychological counselling only and require specific (diagnostic) therapeutic skills to address distressing psychological symptoms, such as anxiety, depression, hopelessness, demoralisation, low mood, anger, shame, feeling trapped by the illness and loss of autonomy, identity or roles (e.g. cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) [ , – ], acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT) [ , ], systemic [ ] and hypnotherapeutic interventions [ , ], MBSR [ , – ] and psychodynamic interventions [ , ]); (e) use of psychological interventions to address spiritual/existential distress (e.g. integration of spiritual aspects, meaning [ , , ]- and dignity-centred interventions [ , ], narrative approach [ ], life review approaches [ , ] and logotherapy/existential analysis interventions) [ , ]; (f) use of psychological interventions for distressing social aspects, such as isolation or loneliness, worries about relatives or being a burden to others, financial worries and communication problems with relatives or team members (ethical and psychological counselling, promote successful communication with patients and relatives/in the multiprofessional team, systemic interventions) [ , , ]; (g) use of interventions to prevent prolonged grief disorder (e.g. grief counselling for relatives, meaning- and dignity- centred interventions) [ – ]. Above all, meaning- and dignity-centred therapy, narrative therapy, life story work, existential therapy, systemic therapy and elements thereof can be considered a specific palliative psychological approach . Therefore, the aim of this study is to describe which psychological interventions (PIs) are used by psychologists/psycho-oncologists in palliative care and to what extent professional experience (years working as a psychologist/psycho-oncologist in a palliative care setting), the palliative care setting, and further training in palliative care for psychologists influence the use of specific interventions. Methods Study design A web-based online survey with psychologists/psycho-oncologists working in specialist palliative care settings for adults across Germany. The survey is reported following the Checklist for Reporting the Results of Internet e-Surveys (CHERRIES) [ ]. The first part of these study results was recently published [ ]. Development and pre-testing of the questionnaire Based on the literature and an online focus group discussion [ ] with six experts in palliative psychology, a questionnaire was developed which allowed for different question formats (multiple choice with the option of multiple answers, open and closed questions, filter questions, rating questions and free text fields). Results of the content analysis with deductive category application of the focus group discussion allowed to select a manageable number of PIs that could be considered in the work with palliative patients and their relatives [ ]. The entire survey contained 23 demographic questions, 45 questions on PIs, six questions on professional attitude and five questions on satisfaction facets. After a pre-test and a think-aloud protocol, the questionnaire was optimised [ ]. Recruitment process and description of the sample Psychologists/psycho-oncologists who regularly work with adult patients and their relatives in German palliative care units within hospitals (PCU), palliative care support teams within hospitals (HST), specialist palliative home care (SPHC), inpatient hospices (IH) and psychological/psycho-oncological services or liaison services (POS) working in a consultative manner were invited to participate. All identifiable palliative care facilities and potential psychologists/psycho-oncologists working in specialist palliative care settings throughout Germany were contacted by email, informed about the study and invited to participate. A

satisfaction facets. After a pre-test and a think-aloud protocol, the questionnaire was optimised [ ]. Recruitment process and description of the sample Psychologists/psycho-oncologists who regularly work with adult patients and their relatives in German palliative care units within hospitals (PCU), palliative care support teams within hospitals (HST), specialist palliative home care (SPHC), inpatient hospices (IH) and psychological/psycho-oncological services or liaison services (POS) working in a consultative manner were invited to participate. All identifiable palliative care facilities and potential psychologists/psycho-oncologists working in specialist palliative care settings throughout Germany were contacted by email, informed about the study and invited to participate. A more detailed description of the recruitment process und resulting sample has been described in Scheiner et al. [ ]. Survey administration A personalised access link to the questionnaire was sent to eligible participants via an invitation email from Lime Survey (software platform for web-based surveys) [ ]. Psychologists/psycho-oncologists were informed about data protection at the beginning of the anonymised survey and had to confirm that their participation was voluntary before processing. It was possible to scroll back, take a break or to terminate the questionnaire at any time without giving reasons. The survey was active for six weeks and took place from end of October until mid-December 2023 with a reminder email after four weeks. Description of the variables reported in this article Demographic characteristics: Gender, age, professional experience (PE) = years working as a psychologist/psycho-oncologist in a palliative care setting; degree at Master’s/Diploma level, training and further education, licence to (psychotherapy)practise; palliative setting, hours per week in palliative setting, integration into MPCT, job allocation/job sharing. Self-assessment of the use of PIs: items PI01 to PI45 on a 7-point ordinal Likert scale from never (1) to very often (7), cut-off at 2 = rather rarely, then filter question with 7 response options on a nominal scale (1 = ‘I don’t know’, 2 = ‘not competent enough’, 3 = ‘patients/relatives rarely suitable for it’, 4 = ‘patient usually no longer able to’, 5 = ‘palliative care too short’, 6 = ‘not enough resources’, 7 = ‘other reasons’); if option 7 was selected, the individual reason could be specified in a free text field. Data analysis The data were processed and analysed using IBM SPSS Statistics—Version 29.0.2.0 [20] [ ]. After checking for missing values, influential data points, processing time, conspicuous time stamps and response patterns the raw data was adjusted according to predetermined exclusion criteria. Sample characteristics are reported in mean values, standard deviations, median or valid percentages depending on their scaling level. Response behaviour on the use of PIs (PI01 to PI45) is presented in absolute numbers, valid percentage values, mean values, standard deviations, standard errors of the mean values, median, skewness, kurtosis and range. Response behaviour for filter questions is presented in absolute numbers and the individual reasons from the free text fields are summarized as content-oriented analysis and integrated in the discussion. Intercorrelations between items of interest were calculated as Pearson for metric variables, Spearman (Rho) for ordinal variables and contingency measure Phi for dichotomous variables [ ]. The following procedures were carried out to analyse how PE, predominantly/less working in a palliative setting, and the completion of further training in palliative care for psychologists (PCP) influence the use of specific interventions: a) creation of a dichotomous variable ‘predominantly palliative setting’ (PS) versus ‘less palliative setting’ (coding 0/reference category = less palliative setting, 1/control = PS); included in PS were those who indicated a predominant activity in PCU, SPHC, IH or HST; psychologists/psycho-oncologists who worked in POS, were only included if the POS hours were < than in PCU/HST/SPHC/IH or the hours were equally distributed (between POS and PCU/HST/SPHC/IH), as long as they were more than 10 h; outpatient settings without clear indicated working time were not included; b) theory-driven intuitive scale construction by combining those interventions that can most closely be associated with the (hypno)systemic-integrative approach (PI04, PI07, PI08, PI11, PI12, PI18, PI19, PI20, PI21, PI22, PI23) into ‘(hypno)systemic-integrative’ scale (ordinal 7-point Likert scale) for an ordinal regression using logit-link [ – ]; c) theory-driven intuitive scale construction by combining those interventions that can most closely be classified as meaning-, dignity-centred and existential approaches (PI33, PI34, PI35, PI36, PI37, PI38, PI39, PI40, PI45) into ‘meaning-dignity-existential’ scale [ ]; due to a lack of normal and pronounced right-skewed distribution of these items even after combining them into one scale, the scale was dichotomised despite the risk of information loss [ ] to facilitate interpretable binary logistic regression using enter method (coding 0/reference category = frequency low including never, almost never, rarely, 1/control = frequency high including very often, often, occasionally, rather rarely with an a priori defined cut-off at 3.5 out of 7, based on the conceptual midpoint separating low versus high frequency responses [ ]) [ ,

PI36, PI37, PI38, PI39, PI40, PI45) into ‘meaning-dignity-existential’ scale [ ]; due to a lack of normal and pronounced right-skewed distribution of these items even after combining them into one scale, the scale was dichotomised despite the risk of information loss [ ] to facilitate interpretable binary logistic regression using enter method (coding 0/reference category = frequency low including never, almost never, rarely, 1/control = frequency high including very often, often, occasionally, rather rarely with an a priori defined cut-off at 3.5 out of 7, based on the conceptual midpoint separating low versus high frequency responses [ ]) [ , , ]; d) the variable PCP was coded 0/reference group = no further training in palliative care for psychologists, 1/control = further training in palliative care for psychologists. Imputation of the small proportion of missing values (1.86%) did not appear appropriate for this study design despite missing completely at random (χ 2 (5040) = 4800.818, p = 0.992) [ – ]. Further exploratory analyses did not yield evidence of additional factors associated with the use of psychological interventions. Results Response rates and description of the sample Two hundred ten participants (86.7% female) with an average age of 44.8 years and PE of 6.15 years completed the questionnaire (view rate 57.3%, participation rate 85.5%, completion rate 87.1%), see Fig. and Table . A small proportion (17.6%) had completed PCP, while 79% had undertaken further training in psycho-oncology. Half of the sample worked in a predominantly palliative setting and 57.1% were firmly integrated into a MPCT. Participants were most frequently employed both in a PCU and in the POS (36.7%), followed by employment in the POS (17.1%) or the PCU (15.2%) exclusively. Psychological interventions Exact wording and response behaviour of the participants on the use of PIs (PI01 to PI45) can be seen in Table . Table provides a more detailed analysis of the items. Low-threshold and rather non-specific interventions like resource collection, psychological counseling, crisis intervention or psychoeducation showed a strong tendency towards agreement (left-skewed) and little discriminatory power, as not all seven response categories were used. Interventions from the fields of systemic therapy and counselling, MBSR, specific psycho-oncological interventions, ethical counselling or body psychotherapy methods were in the middle range. Interventions of the meaning-, dignity- and existential approach were particularly right skewed and discriminated between the respondents to a limited extent. Table provides an overview of categories of similarly frequently used interventions. Influence of professional experience, palliative care setting and further training in palliative care for psychologists on the use of (hypno)systemic-integrative interventions As an intermediate step a theory-driven intuitive scale was calculated (see Appendix B—Table) from the mean values of the items PI04, PI07, PI08, PI11, PI12, PI18, PI19, PI20, PI21, PI22 and PI23 ( M = 4.53, MIC = 0.220, Cronbach’s α = 0.761). The data for the ordinal regression analysis met the assumptions of independent observations, no perfect multicollinearity and parallelism [−2 Log-Likelihood = 980.342, χ2(141) = 119.114, p = 909]. The statistically significant model [χ2(3) = 30.481, p < 0.001], with high goodness of fit [Pearson χ2(3021) = 2693.376, p > 0.05; deviation measure χ2(3021) = 895.147, p > 0.05] explained low proportion of variance (Nagelkerke’s R 2 = 0.140) (see Fig. and Appendix C—Table). Higher PE increased the probability (OR = 1.147, CI [1.088, 1.209]) of being classified in a higher rating category of the utilisation of (hypno)systemic-integrative interventions, with a β = 0.137 ( p < 0.001, 95% CI [0.084, 0.190]). PCP and PS showed no significant influence. Influence of professional experience, palliative care setting and further training in palliative care for psychologists on the use of meaning-dignity-existential interventions As an intermediate step a theory-driven intuitive scale (see Appendix B—Table) was calculated from the mean values of the items PI33, PI34, PI35, PI36, PI37, PI38, PI39, PI40 and PI45 ( M = 2.65, MIC = 0.325, Cronbach’s α = 0.810). The sample included n = 41 participants who fell into the category ‘meaning-dignity-existential’ high and n = 169 into the category ‘meaning-dignity-existential’ low. The assumptions of independent observations, no perfect multicollinearity and approximately linear relationship between the continuous predictor (PE) and the logit of the outcome were met. meaning-dignity-existential interventions As an intermediate step a theory-driven intuitive scale (see Appendix B—Table) was calculated from the mean values of the items PI33, PI34, PI35, PI36, PI37, PI38, PI39, PI40 and PI45 ( M = 2.65, MIC = 0.325, Cronbach’s α = 0.810). The sample included n = 41 participants who fell into the category ‘meaning-dignity-existential’ high and n = 169 into the category ‘meaning-dignity-existential’ low. The assumptions of independent observations, no perfect multicollinearity and approximately linear relationship between the continuous predictor (PE) and the logit of the outcome were met. The statistically significant model [χ2(3) = 10.391, p = 0.02] demonstrated a high level of goodness of fit [Hosmer–Lemeshow test: χ2(8) = 2.883, p > 0.05], but a low level of variance explanation (Nagelkerke’s R 2 = 0.079) and 79.8% correctly classified cases (without predictors 80.3%) (see Fig. and Appendix D—Table). The classification plot with a cut-off at 0.50 showed that cases were incorrectly predicted, particularly in areas with high values on the ‘meaning-dignity-existential’ scale (with a sensitivity of 2.5% and a specificity of 98.8%). Model estimates suggested that, for every additional year of PE, the odds for using ‘meaning-dignity-existential’ interventions are approximately 1.074 higher (CI 95% [1.002, 1.152]). It became also apparent, that the odds for using ‘meaning-dignity-existential’ interventions were for participants with PCP approximately 2.341 higher compared with those without PCP (CI 95% [1.025, 5.349]). Working in a PS showed no significant influence in this sample. Insight into the reasons why interventions were rather rarely, rarely or never used The most common reason (see Appendix E – Table and Appendix H—Figure) given by participants for rather rarely, rarely or never using an intervention was ‘not competent enough’ ( n = 1299). This applied particularly, for example, to ‘catathymic-imaginative psychotherapy’ ( n = 95), ‘trauma therapeutic interventions’ ( n = 93), ‘hypnotherapeutic interventions’ ( n = 84) or ‘manualised meaning-centred interventions CALM/SMiLE/Outlook’ ( n = 55). The second most common reason was ‘I don’t know’ ( n = 1022). This reason was often given for example regarding ‘systemic palliative psychotherapy’ ( n = 121), ‘manualised meaning-centred interventions according to William Breitbart’ ( n = 120), ‘manualised existential psychotherapy’ ( n = 82) or ‘elements of life review approaches’ ( n = 65). Other reasons such as ‘Not enough resources’ ( n = 321) most frequently for ‘manualised dignity-centred therapy’ ( n = 61), ‘Palliative care too short’ ( n = 278) most frequently for ‘manualised dignity-centred therapy’ ( n = 26), ‘Patients/relatives rarely suitable for it’ ( n = 272) most frequently for ‘guideline-based psychological diagnostics/screening’ ( n = 41) and ‘Patient usually no longer able to’ ( n = 193) most frequently for ‘interventions from systemic therapy and counselling’ ( n = 24) were less common. Other reasons from free text fields ( n = 519) resulted in six categories with similar content (‘not my therapeutic attitude/orientation’, ‘not my job/someone else does it’, ‘not familiar with’, ‘not necessary/not required’, ‘not suitable in this setting’, ‘lack of resources/inappropriate structures’) and are summarized in Appendix F—Table. Discussion Key findings To our knowledge, this is the first Germany-wide survey of psychologists and psycho-oncologists investigating the use and evaluation of psychological interventions in palliative care. Even if these results cannot be generalised and applied to other countries, they nevertheless provide a useful overview of how frequently different psychological interventions are used and why certain interventions are used less often (see Table ). The most frequently used interventions include e.g. explorative diagnostics without guidelines, resource collection, psychological counselling, exploration of previous coping strategies, crisis intervention, or psychoeducation. Least frequently used were e.g. manualised existential psychotherapy, manualised meaning-centred interventions according to Breitbart, manualised dignity-centred therapy, manualised life review approaches or elements of meaning-centred interventions. Methods such as promoting successful communication within the MPCT, MBSR interventions, behavioural therapy elements or systemic therapy interventions and counselling were in the middle range and were used occasionally, rather rarely or rarely. In summary, our findings indicate that interventions from a specific palliative psychological approach were used less frequently compared with non-specific interventions than expected and recommended. The most common reason was a lack of familiarity with such interventions, a lack of confidence in their ability to perform them competently or insufficient resources. Compared to the meaning-, dignity-centred and existential interventions, those from the (hypno)systemic-integrative approach appear to be more common yet were still used less frequently than expected. The most common reasons given for this were that participants either did not feel competent enough in this area, or that they had the impression that patients were no longer capable of participating or that palliative care was too short. Having longer professional experience in palliative care, as well as further training in palliative care for psychologists, increased the likelihood of meaning-dignity-existential interventions being used. The use of (hypno)systemic-integrative

them competently or insufficient resources. Compared to the meaning-, dignity-centred and existential interventions, those from the (hypno)systemic-integrative approach appear to be more common yet were still used less frequently than expected. The most common reasons given for this were that participants either did not feel competent enough in this area, or that they had the impression that patients were no longer capable of participating or that palliative care was too short. Having longer professional experience in palliative care, as well as further training in palliative care for psychologists, increased the likelihood of meaning-dignity-existential interventions being used. The use of (hypno)systemic-integrative interventions only increased with longer professional experience. Discussion of the descriptive results The most frequently used interventions can best be classified as general, low-threshold and non-specific. This type of interventions was also predominantly identified by psychologists in a German palliative hospital support team in 2024 [ ]. This seems insofar plausible as this is an approach that is needs-oriented, resource-oriented, situation-adapted, and which is also recommended for this setting [ , ]. A survey from Spain [ ] reported also the use of interventions that were primarily non-specific and rather general in nature, like coping/adapting with the illness and the situation, integration of spiritual aspects or supporting communication between patients and their relatives. Specific meaning- and dignity-centred interventions or interventions from systemic counselling and therapy were probably not mentioned or named at the time (2008) due to a lack of awareness. In the UK, palliative psychologists mentioned specific palliative psychological approaches only in passing and played a subordinate role or were not reported at all [ , ]. Another study described that interventions particularly suited to palliative care were unknown to the majority of the participants [ ]. Among other things, the authors of the aforementioned studies conclude that greater consideration should be given to the specific needs in palliative care settings and that targeted interventions and approaches designed for this purpose should be integrated and evaluated [ , , , ]. Given these long-standing conclusions and recommendations, it is noteworthy that meaning- and dignity-centred interventions were still little known and used relatively rarely in our study. The unsystematic research in this area and calls for specifying exactly what kind of psychological interventions were involved, who was conducting them or how symptoms were identified has been criticised [ ]. Madl et al.’s proposal for psycho-oncology to develop a taxonomy of intervention techniques could be very useful for this purpose [ ]. Such a comprehensive and structured taxonomy of palliative psychological intervention methods could lead to a common standard, facilitating care and efficacy research and increase the construct and content validity of a future survey. At the same time, it will probably remain challenging to operationalise the work of palliative psychologists in the same way as in other psychological or psychotherapeutic settings with standardised or manualised procedures. For this reason, several authors recommend tailoring and modifying the range of interventions to the needs and resources of those affected [ , , , , , ]. Strada has developed a comprehensive framework for palliative psychology and offers useful guidance on this topic [ ]. Such a framework concept based on evidence and expert knowledge that provides practitioners with practical guidelines would be an important and desirable step towards ensuring appropriate and comparable psychological support at the end of life. Implementing such recommendations and framework conditions could help make the training of psychologists and psycho-oncologists more targeted and clarify the remit of palliative care institutions with regard to palliative psychological support. Furthermore, it remains unclear to what extent the utilisation behaviour of those affected influences the use and evaluation of the interventions, as this could not be considered in this study. This potentially depends on patients’ perceived distress and need, attitudes toward psychological care, personality traits and sociodemographic factors, as well as on clinicians’ recommendations, information provision, and structural accessibility of services [ – ]. In light of the substantial evidence and recommendations for the targeted use of meaning- and dignity-centred interventions with seriously ill and dying patients [ , , , ], the findings of this study prompt the question as to why such interventions remain underutilised and relatively unknown. Wishes for hasten death are a common symptom of psychological and existential distress experienced at the end of life [ ]. They are often caused and perpetuated by feelings of loss of dignity, meaning, hope or autonomy, or by feeling like a burden to others [ , , ]. Meaning- and dignity-centred interventions can alleviate not only existential distress but also reduce wishes for hasten death [ , , – ]. In view of the rising number of assisted dying [ , ], such psychological interventions should be promoted and employed much more strongly as an effective contribution to successful suicide prevention

hasten death are a common symptom of psychological and existential distress experienced at the end of life [ ]. They are often caused and perpetuated by feelings of loss of dignity, meaning, hope or autonomy, or by feeling like a burden to others [ , , ]. Meaning- and dignity-centred interventions can alleviate not only existential distress but also reduce wishes for hasten death [ , , – ]. In view of the rising number of assisted dying [ , ], such psychological interventions should be promoted and employed much more strongly as an effective contribution to successful suicide prevention in the palliative care context. Discussion of the inferential results One possible explanation for the underrepresentation of interventions from a specific palliative psychological approach is a lack of relevant professional experience in palliative care and further training in palliative care for psychologists. This can potentially be interpreted as confirmation that a targeted knowledge transfer on dealing with serious physical illnesses, dying, death and grief continue to play a subordinate role within the field of psychology and psychotherapy [ ]. It may also reflect a predominantly deficit-oriented focus on coping with declining physical and mental functioning. Existential concerns, particularly those related to dignity, meaning-making, and living in the face of death, remain comparatively neglected. Our sample showed that psychologists/psycho-oncologists with increased professional experience in palliative care and further training in palliative care for psychologists were more likely to use interventions centred on meaning, dignity and existential issues. For the more frequent use of (hypno)systemic-integrative methods, this only applied to those with longer professional experience. The finding that specialist training and professional experience seem to be essential for the perception and shaping of one’s own role and thus also influence the choice and use of interventions confirms previous research [ , , , ]. Overall, these findings provide valuable information for potential palliative psychologists, can contribute to raising awareness among relevant stakeholders as well as educational institutions and serve as a valuable resource for future research projects. Uniform documentation of psychological consultations could serve as a quality indicator, unfold a positive effect on users themselves, in terms of self-reflection and learning from one another, but also on other professional groups [ ]. This could help to make the work of palliative psychologists more transparent. Strengths and limitations When interpreting the present results, the limitations of this study must also be considered. Although more than 200 [ ] psychologists in Germany have completed further training in palliative care for psychologists, 134 [ ] are currently certified as specialist psychologists for palliative care and 142 [ ] registered with the German Society for Palliative Medicine psychology section, these figures are not reflected in the present study. As it was not possible to identify and examine the entire population of palliative psychologists in Germany, the extent to which the results are biased by participant self-selection remains unclear. It also remains unclear whether certain groups of psychologists/psycho-oncologists were not included because of the recruitment method. Accordingly, it is conceivable that those who could not be reached might have different levels of professional experience and qualification profiles and therefore different intervention preferences. We have addressed this obstacle by conducting an extensive search and contacting all identifiable institutions and potential psychologists/psycho-oncologists. Although the focus group discussion enabled a significant reduction of psychological interventions in the questionnaire (Appendix G – Figure), completion still took quite a long time which could have led to premature termination. Future studies of this kind should favour a more economical survey method. At the same time, this limitation and selection may also have led to important interventions not being considered. Even though our questions were formulated in such a way that the interventions surveyed could be used for both patients and relatives, it was left up to the participants to decide which of these two groups they referred to in each case. Future studies could benefit from focusing on one of the two target groups, as the repertoire of interventions is likely to differ in some respects. The interpretation of the results is further limited by the operationalisation of the variables of interest and the retrospective decision to use theory-driven intuitive scale construction for the inferential statistical analyses. In addition, valuable information may have been lost due to the scale ‘meaning-dignity-existential’ being dichotomised [ ]. However, this approach appeared to be unavoidable, given the distribution of the data and a lack of suitable taxonomy. Methodological and statistical decisions also limit the generalisability of our results and interpretations. Given the heterogeneity and diversity of the qualifications and further training of the study participants other predictors, such as the existence of a licenced training programme, different therapy schools or other types of further training could have been tested (e.g. using multiple hierarchical regression). Predictor selection was

the inferential statistical analyses. In addition, valuable information may have been lost due to the scale ‘meaning-dignity-existential’ being dichotomised [ ]. However, this approach appeared to be unavoidable, given the distribution of the data and a lack of suitable taxonomy. Methodological and statistical decisions also limit the generalisability of our results and interpretations. Given the heterogeneity and diversity of the qualifications and further training of the study participants other predictors, such as the existence of a licenced training programme, different therapy schools or other types of further training could have been tested (e.g. using multiple hierarchical regression). Predictor selection was theory-driven, based on the assumption that in the German context, specific training in palliative care may be more relevant for palliative psychological practice than other forms of professional training. Other qualifications (e.g. psychotherapy licensure) were analysed only exploratively and did not appear to influence intervention choice. Future research should examine these associations in greater detail. Despite its shortcomings, this survey has succeeded in offering valuable insights into palliative psychological work and thus has successfully closed this research gap at a national level. Conclusion Low-threshold, needs- and resource-oriented psychological interventions are certainly effective and widely used to help palliative patients and their informal carers to better cope with physical, psychological, social, and spiritual distress. However, interventions specifically designed to address and alleviate existential distress, by strengthening the sense of dignity, fostering meaning, or providing comfort in inconsolable situations, seem to be comparatively less well known and thus less frequently applied. Existential suffering at the end of life can be caused and perpetuated by mental health conditions, but it is also often a reaction to the loss of dignity, meaning, hope, autonomy, control, or the inability to fulfil important roles. To respond to this type of psychospiritual suffering in a helpful and appropriate manner, psychologists and psycho-oncologists require a repertoire of interventions that enable those affected to (re)view themselves and their lives with dignity, meaning and coherence. Approaches such as life review, meaning- and dignity-centred interventions, logotherapy, existential analysis and systemic and hypnotherapeutic methods are suitable for alleviating precisely these aspects of suffering. More frequent use of these interventions would benefit not only patients and their relatives, but also practitioners. By focusing on aspects that broaden our understanding of the value and meaning of lived and remaining life, psychological care would act in the spirit of Cicely Saunders: ‘You matter because you are you, and you matter to the last moment of your life’ [ ]. It would contribute to a core value at the heart of palliative care and holistic medicine. Supplementary Information Supplementary Material 1.
